documents.title: LGD Retail SME workout RDS documentation

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This document describes the construction, content, representativeness and data quality of the reference data set (RDS) for version 2.0 of the LGD model for retail SME exposures (LGD-SME-RET, model identifier MDL-05), which is developed as a material change of the current production version 1.4. The RDS serves the estimation and calibration of the performing LGD, including the collateral haircuts, the BMKB guarantee component and the downturn LGD, and of the ELBE and LGD in-default for the A-IRB own funds calculation. The scope of application covers retail exposures to small and medium-sized enterprises and self-employed clients booked by the Bank in the Netherlands (sole proprietors, partnerships, private limited companies), where the total exposure of the group of connected clients does not exceed EUR 1 million, comprising current account credit facilities, term loans and business mortgage loans. The document follows the RDS template of MRM-STD-021 Annex A (v3.0); template sections that do not apply are retained with the statement "Not applicable" and a justification, and added sections follow the last template section of their chapter. The data description of version 1.4 was part of the legacy MDD v1.4 (2023); this is the first RDS documentation of MDL-05 under the new template.

sections.heading: Observation period
sections.text: The RDS contains all default events of in-scope facilities with a date of default between 1 January 2010 and 31 December 2025 (16 years), with recovery cash flows, costs and status observed up to the cut-off date of 31 December 2026. The unit of observation is the credit facility; recoveries and costs booked at obligor level in the workout system are allocated to facilities as described in section 4.4. After the treatments in chapter 4 the RDS holds 21,698 default events on 21,698 facilities of 12,180 unique obligors, with 1,412,300 facility-months of cash-flow records. Of these, 19,870 (91.6%) relate to closed recovery processes and 1,828 (8.4%) to incomplete processes, mainly defaults of 2023 to 2025. The period exceeds the five-year minimum of CRR Article 181(2) for retail LGD, consists of consecutive years up to the most recent complete default year and includes all relevant internal loss data available. Version 1.4 was calibrated on defaults of 2010–2021; version 2.0 adds the defaults of 2022–2025.

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: The window starts in January 2010 because facility-level recovery data for SME workouts are available in the workout system RECOV only from the migration of SME workout cases in December 2009; earlier recovery data are held at obligor level without cost information. The window covers the aftermath of the financial crisis, the euro area crisis with the peak in Dutch business bankruptcies in 2013, the recovery of 2015–2019, the COVID-19 period with government support measures in 2020–2021 and the rise in bankruptcies in 2023–2025 after the end of support and the repayment of deferred taxes. It therefore contains a representative mix of good and bad years and includes the downturn period DP-B identified in the MDD, so that the long-run average is representative of long-run experience. The economic and legal conditions in the window are relevant for current and foreseeable conditions; the introduction of the Act on the confirmation of extrajudicial restructuring plans (WHOA) in 2021 is analysed in section 5.1.3. With 21,698 defaults, of which 7,154 closed liquidations with collateral realisation, the sample is sufficient for robust estimation in all three calibration segments; the smallest LGD pool contains 486 defaults. Defaults under the definition of default implemented on 1 December 2020 are included from that date, and the window is extended annually so that the share of defaults under the current definition increases; the related MoC is reassessed at each extension.

sections.heading: Default cohorts and status of recovery processes
sections.text: Annex B, table B.1 shows per default year the number of defaults, the share of closed processes and the average realised LGD of defaults that are closed or have reached the maximum recovery period. Default counts rise from 1,540 in 2010 to a peak of 2,120 in 2013, fall to 760 in 2021 and rise again to 1,608 in 2025, reflecting the business bankruptcy cycle. A recovery process is closed when the facility has returned to non-defaulted status, has been fully repaid, when all collateral has been realised and the residual claim written off or settled, or when the maximum recovery period of 72 months after default has been exceeded; closure is recorded without delay in the monthly RDS update. The maximum recovery period of 72 months is supported by the recovery pattern of closed processes: 97.9% of discounted recoveries of closed liquidation cases are received within 72 months, and bankruptcy proceedings with a trustee account for most of the remainder. For the 1,828 incomplete processes, observed cash flows up to the cut-off date are retained and future recoveries are estimated in the MDD from the recovery patterns of closed processes with the same time in default, collateral type and workout phase, applying a conservative percentile. Default years are reported separately and not merged, so that the impact analysis can use as many data points as available.

sections.heading: Target variable and outcome horizon
sections.text: Not applicable in the sense of the template condition: the target is the realised LGD of the regulatory default event defined in section 3.3, measured over the full recovery process up to closure or the maximum recovery period of 72 months, without a fixed 12-month horizon. Component targets are the cure outcome, the realised recovery per collateral type relative to the collateral value at default (recovery-to-value), the realised recovery on the unsecured part and the BMKB claim payment relative to the guaranteed amount. All targets are derived from the same default events, so that the same definition of default applies to the performing LGD, the ELBE and the LGD in-default, and to the observations used by the retail SME PD model MDL-04 for the overlapping period. For defaulted exposures, additional targets are defined per reference date in default (section 4.4.3).

sections.heading: Deviations from the Bank's definition of default
sections.text: For default events between 1 January 2010 and 31 December 2015, the default flag is approximated, because the components of the current definition have been captured in the source systems only since 1 January 2016 (CR-STD-110 section 9.3). For this period a default is set when the arrears on any facility of the obligor exceed EUR 100 and 1% of the total exposure at three consecutive month-ends, or when the SME arrears system records a bankruptcy, a suspension of payments, a WSNP registration, a transfer to FR&R with a restructuring or a specific provision. On the 2016–2019 overlap period the approximation identifies 95.9% of the defaults of the reconstructed current definition and generates 3.4% additional defaults, and the average realised LGD of the approximated set is 0.6 percentage points lower. Probation periods cannot be reconstructed for 2010–2015; a return to non-default is recognised after three consecutive month-ends without arrears above the threshold and without an FR&R case, which is recorded as data deficiency DD-LGDS-01 and covered by MoC component A1. From January 2016 to November 2020 the flag is reconstructed from daily data with the current definition, and from 1 December 2020 the production flag under CR-STD-110 v2.0 is used; the three definitions are analysed separately in Annex B, table B.4. The regulatory materiality threshold has been applied since 1 December 2020, the date of application set by De Nederlandsche Bank, and the RDS field DEF_FLAG_SOURCE identifies for every event which definition applies.

sections.heading: Default definition
sections.text: A default occurs when the obligor is more than 90 consecutive days past due on a material credit obligation or is considered unlikely to pay, in accordance with CRR Article 178 and CR-STD-110. Days past due are counted from the first day on which both the absolute component of EUR 100 and the relative component of 1% of the retail materiality threshold are exceeded, and counting restarts when either component is no longer exceeded. The absolute component is compared with the sum of all past due amounts of the obligor to the Bank and its subsidiaries, and the relative component divides that sum by the obligor's total on-balance-sheet exposure, excluding equity exposures. The relative threshold of 1% is the level set by De Nederlandsche Bank; no lower internal threshold is used as UTP indication. The obligor is defaulted when both components are exceeded for 90 consecutive days, with the default flag activated at the onset of the 91st day; for current account facilities, an overdrawn limit counts as past due from the first day of the excess. Days past due are computed daily in the SME arrears system (SAMS), and the date of default, the first day on which any criterion is met, is recorded for every event in DEF_DATE. Once the past due criterion is met the obligor is classified as defaulted without further judgement, unless a technical past due situation is confirmed.

sections.heading: Level of application, joint obligations and contagion
sections.text: Default is applied at obligor level for all retail SME exposures, consistent with the Bank's practice of managing SME clients as a single relationship; the level of application has not changed over the observation period. All credit obligations of a defaulted obligor, including private mortgages of a sole proprietor held by the Bank, are flagged as defaulted in all relevant systems. Partnerships (vof) and their partners are connected: the default of the partnership is propagated to the partners' exposures, as partners are jointly and severally liable, and joint obligations are treated as separate obligors in the materiality threshold calculation. Contagion within groups of connected clients (for example an operating company and its holding company) is specified in the connected clients procedure CC-PRC-02: default of an operating company leads to default of the holding when the holding's income depends on it for more than 50%; other cases are assessed individually by FR&R. The same definition of default is used by all Group entities with retail SME exposures in the Netherlands.

sections.heading: Counting of days past due
sections.text: Any amount of principal, interest or fee not paid when due, and any excess over the approved current account limit, is recognised as past due. Where the payment schedule has been modified, days past due are counted on the modified schedule, and each modification granted because of financial difficulties is assessed for distressed restructuring. Instalments deferred under the COVID-19 payment deferral scheme of 2020 were not counted as past due; the reasons for deferral were analysed, and 612 obligors were assessed as unlikely to pay. Counting is suspended for disputed amounts only where the dispute is before a court or Kifid. Technical past due is recognised only for errors of Bank systems, payment system failures and payment allocation time lags; each case is documented, corrected within 30 days and reviewed quarterly by Credit Risk Management. The policies on re-ageing, extensions, renewals of current account limits and netting of accounts are set in the SME arrears procedure SAMS-PRC-03 v2.4; renewal of an overdrawn limit without a credit decision is not permitted. The 640 technical past due events identified in the RDS are removed from the defaulted exposures used for estimation.

sections.heading: Return to non-defaulted status and multiple defaults
sections.text: An obligor returns to non-defaulted status only when no default trigger applies anymore, after a probation period of at least three months and an assessment by FR&R that the improvement is factual and permanent, based on recent financial statements and account behaviour. After a distressed restructuring, including WHOA restructuring plans, the probation period is at least 12 months from the latest of the restructuring, the default classification and the end of any grace period, and requires a material payment, no past due amounts and no doubt about full repayment. The probation start date and status are recorded for every default event. A facility that defaults again within 12 months of returning to non-defaulted status is treated as continuously defaulted from the first default; the period exceeds the nine months of EBA/GL/2017/16 paragraph 101 and is justified by the observation that 76% of SME re-defaults occur within 12 months. Default events are linked by DEF_CHAIN_ID; 1,560 events were merged into a preceding default, as listed in Annex B, table B.6, with all cash flows of both events included in the economic loss of the first.

sections.heading: Unlikeliness-to-pay triggers
sections.text: Non-accrued status, specific credit risk adjustments including IFRS 9 Stage 3, sale of a credit obligation at a credit-related loss above 5%, distressed restructuring with a diminished financial obligation above 1%, bankruptcy, suspension of payments or WSNP of the obligor, and the forced sale of collateral lead to default automatically. Facilities on which interest is no longer recognised because of a decline in credit quality are non-accrued and defaulted. Specific credit risk adjustments resulting from a significant decline in credit quality are UTP indications, collective Stage 1 and 2 allowances are not, and all Stage 3 exposures are defaulted. For every forbearance measure the diminished financial obligation (NPV0 - NPV1)/NPV0 is calculated at the original effective interest rate, and exposures above 1% are defaulted; forborne exposures below the threshold are assessed for a large final instalment, irregular schedules, grace periods and repeated forbearance, and all forborne non-performing exposures are defaulted. No SME credit obligations were sold in the observation period; a future sale would be assessed for the credit-related loss L = (E - P)/E against the threshold of 5%.

sections.heading: Additional indications and identification process
sections.text: Additional UTP indicators for SME exposures are a significant decline in turnover or cash flow, breach of financial covenants, negative equity in the annual accounts, tax arrears reported by the Tax Administration, fraud and a second forbearance request within 24 months; they lead to a case-by-case assessment by FR&R within 30 days of detection, whose outcome and rationale are recorded. External information used includes the Chamber of Commerce register, the Central Insolvency Register, BKR for sole proprietors, credit bureau alerts and sector news from Credit Risk Management's watch process. For each indication the identification method, information sources and monitoring frequency are defined in Annex A, table A.3, which maps each trigger to its source-system fields, and the operationalisation of each trigger is described in the SME default handbook DoD-HB-SME v1.8. Automatic triggers are identified daily by SAMS, manual triggers from watch lists, forbearance lists and specific provisions at least weekly, and all exposures of a defaulted obligor are flagged in all systems within one business day. Forborne non-performing exposures are verified monthly to be defaulted, and forborne performing exposures are reviewed quarterly for UTP indications. To ensure consistent labelling of judgement-based UTP flags, FR&R applies guideline UTP-GL-SME-01, and Credit Risk Management re-assesses a sample of 120 cases each year; agreement in 2026 was 95.8%.

sections.heading: Consistency of the default definition
sections.text: The same definition of default is used for the IRB approach, IFRS 9 Stage 3, non-performing exposure reporting and credit risk management, and forms the basis for SME credit monitoring and management reporting. The default triggers are implemented identically across SAMS, the SME lending platform and the Group's data warehouse, and completeness of default identification is reconciled monthly between SAMS and the default register. The RDS default flag is constructed in accordance with CR-STD-110 and is consistent with CRR Article 178; for 2021–2025 it matches the production default flag for 99.5% of events, the differences being explained by retroactive technical past due corrections. The IRB and IFRS 9 default flags are reconciled quarterly between the risk and finance systems. The register of default definitions maintained by Credit Risk Management records scope, approving body and date, implementation date, changes, change category and supervisory dates for every version. The prudential default flag and the accounting Stage 3 flag are labelled distinctly in the Group Data Catalogue.

sections.heading: Data sources and lineage
sections.text: The RDS is built from the SME lending platform (BLP), the SME arrears system (SAMS), the workout system RECOV, the collateral management system (CMS, since June 2019; legacy system ZEKERHEDEN before), the BMKB guarantee administration and the general ledger. External inputs are the CBS house price index, the MSCI Netherlands commercial property capital value index received quarterly under licence, 3-month EURIBOR fixings and the RVO claim settlement statements for BMKB guarantees. Every RDS variable is traced from source table and field through the credit risk data warehouse to the RDS, with each transformation, filter, join and aggregation referenced to the build code module and the extraction frequency and timing, as documented in Annex A. For each type of risk data an authoritative source is defined (BLP for contract data, SAMS for arrears and defaults, RECOV for recoveries and costs, CMS for collateral, the BMKB administration for guarantees and the general ledger for write-offs). Two manual inputs exist, the mapping of ZEKERHEDEN collateral types to CMS collateral types and the sector mapping of legacy SBI codes, both version-controlled files whose lineage entries identify the four-eyes control applied. The lineage of the migrated collateral data was updated before use, when CMS replaced ZEKERHEDEN in 2019.

sections.heading: Data ownership and metadata
sections.text: The RDS draws on the data domains SME Lending, Credit Risk, Recovery and Collateral, each with exactly one Data Owner in the Group Data Catalogue, and the model data is mapped to these domains. Roles for data ownership and quality are defined for the business and for IT application owners. The model owner agreed data quality expectations for the critical data elements with the Data Owners in DQA-LGDS-2026 of 15 December 2026. Metadata for all RDS data elements are recorded and versioned in the Group Data Catalogue, using the Group identifiers for customers, facilities and collateral objects. Changes to definitions, sources or transformations are approved by the Data Owner and announced to the model owner in advance through the data change calendar. These arrangements implement the Bank's data governance under DATA-POL-001 for all model inputs.

sections.heading: Exclusions
sections.text: From 24,310 default events of facilities in the retail SME segment, 1,560 were merged into preceding defaults (section 3.3.3), leaving 22,750 events; the following exclusions, each approved by the model owner, were then applied. E1 technical past due: 640 events (2.8% of events; 0.6% of outstanding amount at default), removed because they are not defaults under CR-STD-110. E2 facilities outside the range of application at default: 412 events (1.8%; 6.9% of outstanding amount) of obligors whose group exposure exceeded EUR 1 million at default and which were therefore treated in the corporate rating system, whose LGD model covers them. No exclusion exceeds 5% of records in any segment; E2 exceeds 5% of the outstanding amount at default and was therefore approved by the model owner and reported to Model Validation on 18 February 2027. The conclusion of the impact analysis in section 5.3 is that E1 lowers and E2 has no material effect on the long-run average LGD. All other defaults observed in the observation period within the scope of the model are included in the LGD quantification.

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: Missing values are treated per variable as documented in Annex C, distinguishing values missing at random, for structural reasons and because of data deficiencies. The main case is the valuation date of collateral migrated from ZEKERHEDEN, missing for 11.2% of collateral objects of defaults before 2019 (data deficiency DD-LGDS-02); for these objects the date of the last credit review is used, which is conservative as it leads to a larger indexation adjustment. Sector code is missing for 0.9% of obligors (missing at random) and is set to the sector group 'other services'; imputations are reproducible in module impute_sme.py and the shares are reported in Annex C. Outliers are identified with documented criteria applied identically in development and production: collateral value above 20 times the exposure, time in default above 150 months and costs above 30% of the outstanding amount; collateral coverage is capped at 5 (212 facilities), which changes the LRA LGD by less than 0.01 percentage points. Missing values and outliers of the target variable and its constituents are not imputed; 94 records with missing cost booking dates were corrected at source.

sections.heading: Calculation of realised LGD
sections.text: Realised LGD is calculated per facility as economic loss divided by the outstanding amount at default, including principal, accrued interest and fees; economic loss equals the outstanding amount at default plus material direct and indirect costs, minus recoveries, with all cash flows after default discounted to the default date. Amounts forgiven before or at default are added to numerator and denominator; interest and fees capitalised before default are included in the outstanding amount, while amounts capitalised after default do not increase the economic loss. Additional drawings after default on current account facilities are included in the economic loss and not in the conversion factor, in line with CRM-STD-100 section 10.2, and therefore do not increase the outstanding amount at default in the denominator. Recoveries and costs booked in RECOV at obligor level are allocated to the obligor's facilities in proportion to the outstanding amount at default, except collateral proceeds, which are allocated to the facilities secured by that collateral according to the CMS allocation key. All recoveries, costs and additional drawings are discounted with the 3-month EURIBOR at the date of default plus 5 percentage points, the fixing being used as observed including negative values. For cured facilities an artificial cash flow equal to the outstanding amount at the date of return is included and discounted like observed cash flows; realised LGDs below zero are retained unfloored in the RDS.

sections.heading: Direct and indirect costs
sections.text: Direct costs comprise external legal fees, bankruptcy trustee fees, valuation and auction costs, and collection agency fees, booked per case in RECOV and reconciled to the general ledger. Indirect costs of FR&R and the SME arrears teams are allocated using the Bank's activity-based cost accounting: EUR 1,150 per cured case and EUR 4,820 per liquidation case at 2025 prices, indexed with the CPI. Pre-default collection costs are included for the months in arrears before default unless already in the outstanding amount. All material direct and indirect costs are stored per facility and month, and realised LGD therefore includes all material costs and additional drawings after default, as required by CRM-STD-100 section 9.2. The average realised LGD of cured facilities is 3.4%, reflecting costs and the discounting effect over an average time to cure of 11 months.

sections.heading: Reference dates in default
sections.text: For the ELBE and the LGD in-default, reference dates are defined at 0, 6, 12, 24, 36 and 48 months after default and at the date of the bankruptcy declaration, based on the recovery patterns of closed processes: most cures occur within 12 months, collateral sales between 6 and 30 months, and bankruptcy distributions after 36 months. At each reference date, realised LGD is calculated on the outstanding amount at that date, including fees and interest capitalised before it, with subsequent cash flows discounted to that date. The RDS stores for every defaulted facility the data used to assign it to an LGD pool in the year before default, the estimated LGD and the realised LGD. The RDS also stores for each reference date the outstanding amount, the time in default, the workout phase, the collateral values and the BMKB claim status.

sections.heading: Collateral data
sections.text: Collateral data are recorded in CMS with type, value, valuation date and method, lien or pledge rank and the allocation to secured facilities, meeting the data quality requirements of MRM-STD-022. Commercial real estate is valued by independent certified valuers at origination and revalued at least annually, residential property of entrepreneurs at least every three years with statistical indexation in between, and receivables and inventory through periodic pledge lists (monthly for limits above EUR 250,000, otherwise from the annual accounts). Immovable property is valued by qualified valuers independent of the credit decision, at or below market value, with the valuation reduced for prior-ranking claims. Equipment and vehicles are valued at market value, determined by independent appraisal for objects above EUR 250,000 and otherwise from book values adjusted with the appraisal-based ratio per object class. Collateral values used as drivers are taken at the reference date twelve months before default and at default, the earlier value being used where a revaluation shortly before default reflects credit deterioration. For second-ranking mortgages on the entrepreneur's private residence (37% of residential collateral) the prior-ranking claim is deducted, reflecting the subordinated position. Collateral not meeting CRR Article 181(1)(f), such as personal guarantees of directors, is not used as a driver; cash flows from it are recoveries without collateral, with their source recorded.

sections.heading: Economic indicator data
sections.text: Economic indicators used for the downturn identification are stored with source, delivery date and version: GDP, unemployment and business bankruptcies from CBS, write-offs on loans to domestic non-financial SMEs from DNB statistics, gross value added per sector from CBS, and commercial property capital and rental value indices from MSCI. These official and licensed series are considered accurate and reliable; their revisions are tracked. As the exposures are located in the Netherlands, each indicator is included once at national level; sector value added is included for each sector group with more than 10% of EAD (construction, wholesale and retail trade, hospitality, business services, agriculture). Regional commercial property indices were considered but not acquired, as regional series start only in 2015 and the cost is disproportionate to their information value for the portfolio.

sections.heading: Representativeness
sections.text: Representativeness of the RDS for the current portfolio is assessed separately for risk differentiation (driver distributions) and risk quantification (loss levels), with the tests and thresholds of CRM-STD-100 section 6.5 and MV-HB-003 section 6. The analysis covers scope of application, definition of default, distribution of risk characteristics, lending standards and recovery policies, as detailed in Annex B. The scope of the RDS equals the range of application of version 2.0; the definition of default differs only for 2010–2015, for which the effect is quantified and covered by MoC. The RDS is representative of the current portfolio in risk drivers and loss levels, with the explained shifts reported in sections 5.1.1 and 5.1.2. The data used to develop the model are therefore representative, of adequate quality and sufficient in length and depth.

sections.heading: Representativeness of risk-driver distributions
sections.text: Driver distributions in the RDS, measured twelve months before default, were compared with the performing portfolio at 31 December 2025 using the PSI with ten buckets: collateral coverage 0.07, sector group 0.05, legal form 0.04, current account utilisation 0.11, arrears history 0.06, BMKB flag 0.02. The amber PSI for utilisation is explained by the lower average utilisation after 2021, when clients reduced their use of credit lines; the RDS covers the full range of utilisation with at least 900 defaults per bucket. As utilisation is a risk driver of the model and each range is represented, no bias results and no additional sample restriction or driver is needed. The share of other physical collateral located outside the Netherlands is 2.3% in the current portfolio and 1.9% in the RDS.

sections.heading: Representativeness of loss levels
sections.text: Loss levels were compared per calibration segment between the RDS and recent defaults: the realised LGD of closed processes of 2023–2025 defaults (26.1%) is close to the LRA (27.7%), and the two-sample tests of cure rates per segment show no significant difference. Comparability of the data for the long-run average was analysed for scope, default definition, risk characteristics, current and foreseeable economic conditions, and lending and recovery standards. Recovery-to-value ratios of commercial real estate in 2023–2025 (60.8%) are within the range observed over 2010–2025 (52%–66%).

sections.heading: Lending standards, recovery policies and legal environment
sections.text: Changes over the observation period were analysed by comparing RDS data before and after each change: the tightening of collateral requirements for business mortgages in 2014 (maximum LTV 80%), the centralisation of SME workout in FR&R in 2016, the migration to CMS in 2019 and the introduction of the WHOA in January 2021. After 2016, cure rates increased by 3.2 percentage points and time to recovery decreased by 4 months, which is reflected by the inclusion of these defaults in the estimates. WHOA restructurings (48 defaults since 2021) show lower recoveries for unsecured creditors than informal restructurings; the effect is not yet quantifiable with sufficient data and is covered by MoC component B1. Changes in the BMKB scheme, including the temporary BMKB-C variant of 2020–2021, are covered by MoC component B2.

sections.heading: Representativeness for other uses
sections.text: The LGD components are used for IFRS 9 ECL of the SME portfolio and in the SME pricing tool; both uses concern the same population as the RDS. For IFRS 9 the best estimate components without downturn adjustment, MoC and floors are used with forward-looking scenarios, as documented in chapter 1 of the MDD. The model is not used for corporate exposures or for exposures of other Group entities, which lie outside the range of application. Any use outside the RDS population would require a representativeness analysis before extension, as defined in the change procedure.

sections.heading: Impact of exclusions
sections.text: The effect of each exclusion on risk-driver distributions and realised LGD was quantified on the 22,750 events before exclusions. E1 (technical past due) has no effect on driver distributions (PSI 0.01) and would lower the LRA LGD by 0.2 percentage points if retained. E2 (obligors above EUR 1 million) concerns larger obligors with more real estate collateral; their inclusion would lower the LRA LGD by 0.4 percentage points, so the exclusion is conservative. The aggregate effect of all exclusions on the long-run average LGD is +0.6 percentage points (conservative) and was reported to Model Validation with the RDS.

sections.heading: Data quality assessment
sections.text: The data quality assessment of the RDS under MRM-STD-022 is reported in full in EVD-05-DQ; it was performed before estimation on RDS version LGDSME_RDS_v2027.1. All 47 RDS variables, including the 14 candidate risk drivers and the 21 data elements used to construct the target (default flag and date, outstanding amount, recoveries per source, costs, BMKB payments and write-offs), are critical data elements. Data quality was assessed on completeness, accuracy, consistency and timeliness, as well as validity, uniqueness and appropriateness, with 352 rules covering each applicable dimension per element. Thresholds follow MRM-STD-022 section 4.3, with stricter accuracy thresholds of 0.25% and 0.5% for the target constituents. Of the 352 rules, 338 are green, 14 amber and none red; the amber results concern the migrated collateral valuation dates, indirect costs before 2013 and the sector codes of legacy obligors. The assessment concluded that the RDS is fit for the intended use and was signed off by the model developer and the model owner on 19 February 2027, before the RDS was frozen.

sections.heading: Reconciliation, accuracy and controls
sections.text: Outstanding amounts at default were reconciled with BLP (difference 0.18%) and write-offs with the general ledger (0.26%); all default events were reconciled with the default register maintained under CR-STD-110. As MDL-05 is a Tier 2 model, reconciliation and automated rules are the primary accuracy checks; in addition, 150 collateral realisation files were verified against notarial and auction statements because of the collateral data migration. Controls operate from data entry to the RDS, including reconciliations across BLP, SAMS, RECOV, CMS and the general ledger, and the 352 rules are implemented in the Group DQ monitoring tool and applied monthly to the production input data of the LGD engine. Data are aggregated on a largely automated basis; the two manual mappings are documented and controlled. RDS data are reconcilable with accounting data and with COREP exposures of the same reference date. Critical data elements are reconciled with source and accounting data at least annually.

sections.heading: Completeness, consistency and timeliness
sections.text: Record-level completeness was confirmed against the default register and RECOV, and attribute-level completeness is 100% for 36 variables and above 88.8% for all others. Consistency is assessed between the RDS and the production input data, over the observation period including the three default definitions, and between related fields such as collateral sale date and proceeds. Timeliness is measured as the lag between reference date and availability and as the currency of collateral valuations; 4.1% of commercial real estate valuations in the current portfolio are older than the required annual refresh plus one month (amber). Where data are incomplete, the gaps are explained and their effect on the estimates assessed, in particular for the collateral data migrated in 2019. The data are sufficiently precise to avoid distortions of pool assignment and contain no known biases making them unfit for purpose. The DQ dashboard is reported monthly to the model owner and quarterly to the Credit Risk Management Committee.

sections.heading: Data deficiencies
sections.text: Data deficiencies are recorded in the data deficiency log of MDL-05 with identifier, affected variables and segments, dimension, cause, impact and treatment, and each is linked to a margin of conservatism category. DD-LGDS-01: default flag approximated and probation not reconstructable for 2010–2015; impact −0.6 percentage points on LRA; MoC A1; limitations log L-02. DD-LGDS-02: valuation dates missing for 11.2% of migrated collateral objects of pre-2019 defaults and collateral types mapped from ZEKERHEDEN; conservative imputation and MoC A2; limitations log L-03. DD-LGDS-03: indirect costs before 2013 allocated with deflated 2013 unit costs; MoC assessed and included in A1 as the effect is below 0.05 percentage points; limitations log L-04. DD-LGDS-04: sector code missing for 0.9% of obligors; imputation, MoC assessed and rejected. Each deficiency not fully remediated is assessed for inclusion in the MoC as Category A, and the log references the MoC component. DD-LGDS-01 and -02 are permanent historical deficiencies reassessed annually; DD-LGDS-04 has a remediation owner (SME Lending data steward) and target date 30 September 2027, after which the related assessment is repeated.

sections.heading: Expert judgement in data treatment
sections.text: Expert judgement in data treatment is recorded in the expert judgement log EJ-LGDS of MDL-05, which is stored with the model documentation and referenced here and in chapter 11 of the MDD. EJ-LGDS-01 concerns the approximation of the default flag for 2010–2015 and EJ-LGDS-02 the mapping of ZEKERHEDEN collateral types to CMS types; the mapping file is the only manual input to the RDS build and is version controlled. EJ-LGDS-02 addresses data deficiency DD-LGDS-02 and is linked to MoC A2; its log entry records the rationale, the evidence (a comparison of 400 migrated objects with their original deeds), the rejected alternative of treating unmapped objects as unsecured, the impact (−0.3 percentage points on the other-secured LRA), the proposer, approver, approval date, review date and expiry condition. Both judgements are of medium materiality, were challenged by an independent senior modeller and approved by the model owner and the head of development; the proposer was not an approver. The rationale is specific enough to replicate the effect, as the mapping table and the approximation rule are implemented in versioned code.

sections.text: The RDS contains personal data of natural persons, namely sole proprietors, partners and guarantors, processed for development, validation and application of the IRB model on the lawful basis of legal obligation (Article 6(1)(c) GDPR in conjunction with CRR Articles 144 and 179), recorded before processing started. The purposes are specified in the Record of Processing entry RoP-CR-0433, which is referenced in the model inventory record of MDL-05. Reuse of data collected for SME lending is supported by compatibility assessment CA-2025-019 under Article 6(4) GDPR. A DPIA was updated for version 2.0 (DPIA-2026-141, approved 4 December 2026), because personal data of guarantors are newly processed; it describes the processing and purposes, assesses necessity, proportionality and risks, and sets out the mitigating measures, with the advice of the Data Protection Officer documented and a low residual risk. The inventory records that personal data are processed and references the DPIA.

sections.heading: Minimisation, pseudonymisation, retention and fair treatment
sections.text: Personal data attributes are limited to those needed: legal form, sector, account behaviour, collateral and guarantee data; names, addresses and dates of birth of natural persons are not included, and each attribute is justified in Annex A, table A.4 with purpose, lawful basis, pseudonymisation and retention period. Development and validation use pseudonymised data with keyed tokens held by the Data Custodian; re-identification requires Privacy Office approval and is logged, and the RDS is held in the secure analytics environment of Risk with role-based access. Test environments use masked data only, and personal data are kept accurate through the monthly refresh. The frozen RDS is retained for the period of use of the model plus five years, after which personal data are deleted or anonymised with evidence of deletion. No special categories of personal data are processed. Protected attributes (gender, nationality, age) of sole proprietors are excluded, and legal form and sector were screened as potential proxies; correlations with gender and age of sole proprietors are below 0.15, and the results are documented in Annex B, table B.9.

sections.heading: Reproducibility
sections.text: The RDS is built by versioned code in the repository rds-lgd-sme of the Bank's GitLab, tag v2.0.0, from source snapshots extracted on 15 January 2027, in Python 3.11.9 with pandas 2.2.2 and a locked dependency file. All extraction, transformation, exclusion, default flag construction and variable derivation steps are performed by build code without manual data manipulation. A full rebuild by a second developer on 22 February 2027 reproduced the frozen RDS exactly (21,698 default events, 1,412,300 cash-flow records and identical totals of discounted recoveries). The frozen RDS LGDSME_RDS_v2027.1 is stored read-only in the analytics environment, referenced in this document and in the MDD, and was signed off by the model owner on 22 February 2027 before estimation started. The RDS version is archived with its code, lineage and metadata, retained for the life of the model and ten years thereafter, and protected against alteration. Default, loss, recovery and exposure data are retained since 2010, beyond the observation periods required by the CRR. Data, code and documentation supporting the application for the material change remain available, and the RDS remains reproducible, throughout the ECB assessment.

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This document describes the construction, content, representativeness and data quality of the reference data set (RDS) for version 2.0 of the LGD model for retail SME exposures (LGD-SME-RET, model identifier MDL-05), which is developed as a material change of the current production version 1.4. The RDS serves the estimation and calibration of the performing LGD, including the collateral haircuts, the BMKB guarantee component and the downturn LGD, and of the ELBE and LGD in-default for the A-IRB own funds calculation. The scope of application covers retail exposures to small and medium-sized enterprises and self-employed clients booked by the Bank in the Netherlands (sole proprietors, partnerships, private limited companies), where the total exposure of the group of connected clients does not exceed EUR 1 million, comprising current account credit facilities, term loans and business mortgage loans. The document follows the RDS template of MRM-STD-021 Annex A (v3.0); template sections that do not apply are retained with the statement "Not applicable" and a justification, and added sections follow the last template section of their chapter. The data description of version 1.4 was part of the legacy MDD v1.4 (2023); this is the first RDS documentation of MDL-05 under the new template.

sections.heading: Observation period
sections.text: The RDS contains all default events of in-scope facilities with a date of default between 1 January 2010 and 31 December 2025 (16 years), with recovery cash flows, costs and status observed up to the cut-off date of 31 December 2026. The unit of observation is the credit facility; recoveries and costs booked at obligor level in the workout system are allocated to facilities as described in section 4.4. After the treatments in chapter 4 the RDS holds 21,698 default events on 21,698 facilities of 12,180 unique obligors, with 1,412,300 facility-months of cash-flow records. Of these, 19,870 (91.6%) relate to closed recovery processes and 1,828 (8.4%) to incomplete processes, mainly defaults of 2023 to 2025. The period exceeds the five-year minimum of CRR Article 181(2) for retail LGD, consists of consecutive years up to the most recent complete default year and includes all relevant internal loss data available. Version 1.4 was calibrated on defaults of 2010–2021; version 2.0 adds the defaults of 2022–2025.

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: The window starts in January 2010 because facility-level recovery data for SME workouts are available in the workout system RECOV only from the migration of SME workout cases in December 2009; earlier recovery data are held at obligor level without cost information. The window covers the aftermath of the financial crisis, the euro area crisis with the peak in Dutch business bankruptcies in 2013, the recovery of 2015–2019, the COVID-19 period with government support measures in 2020–2021 and the rise in bankruptcies in 2023–2025 after the end of support and the repayment of deferred taxes. It therefore contains a representative mix of good and bad years and includes the downturn period DP-B identified in the MDD, so that the long-run average is representative of long-run experience. The economic and legal conditions in the window are relevant for current and foreseeable conditions; the introduction of the Act on the confirmation of extrajudicial restructuring plans (WHOA) in 2021 is analysed in section 5.1.3. With 21,698 defaults, of which 7,154 closed liquidations with collateral realisation, the sample is sufficient for robust estimation in all three calibration segments; the smallest LGD pool contains 486 defaults. Defaults under the definition of default implemented on 1 December 2020 are included from that date, and the window is extended annually so that the share of defaults under the current definition increases; the related MoC is reassessed at each extension.

sections.heading: Default cohorts and status of recovery processes
sections.text: Annex B, table B.1 shows per default year the number of defaults, the share of closed processes and the average realised LGD of defaults that are closed or have reached the maximum recovery period. Default counts rise from 1,540 in 2010 to a peak of 2,120 in 2013, fall to 760 in 2021 and rise again to 1,608 in 2025, reflecting the business bankruptcy cycle. A recovery process is closed when the facility has returned to non-defaulted status, has been fully repaid, when all collateral has been realised and the residual claim written off or settled, or when the maximum recovery period of 72 months after default has been exceeded; closure is recorded without delay in the monthly RDS update. The maximum recovery period of 72 months is supported by the recovery pattern of closed processes: 97.9% of discounted recoveries of closed liquidation cases are received within 72 months, and bankruptcy proceedings with a trustee account for most of the remainder. For the 1,828 incomplete processes, observed cash flows up to the cut-off date are retained and future recoveries are estimated in the MDD from the recovery patterns of closed processes with the same time in default, collateral type and workout phase, applying a conservative percentile. Default years are reported separately and not merged, so that the impact analysis can use as many data points as available.

sections.heading: Target variable and outcome horizon
sections.text: Not applicable in the sense of the template condition: the target is the realised LGD of the regulatory default event defined in section 3.3, measured over the full recovery process up to closure or the maximum recovery period of 72 months, without a fixed 12-month horizon. Component targets are the cure outcome, the realised recovery per collateral type relative to the collateral value at default (recovery-to-value), the realised recovery on the unsecured part and the BMKB claim payment relative to the guaranteed amount. All targets are derived from the same default events, so that the same definition of default applies to the performing LGD, the ELBE and the LGD in-default, and to the observations used by the retail SME PD model MDL-04 for the overlapping period. For defaulted exposures, additional targets are defined per reference date in default (section 4.4.3).

sections.heading: Deviations from the Bank's definition of default
sections.text: For default events between 1 January 2010 and 31 December 2015, the default flag is approximated, because the components of the current definition have been captured in the source systems only since 1 January 2016 (CR-STD-110 section 9.3). For this period a default is set when the arrears on any facility of the obligor exceed EUR 100 and 1% of the total exposure at three consecutive month-ends, or when the SME arrears system records a bankruptcy, a suspension of payments, a WSNP registration, a transfer to FR&R with a restructuring or a specific provision. On the 2016–2019 overlap period the approximation identifies 95.9% of the defaults of the reconstructed current definition and generates 3.4% additional defaults, and the average realised LGD of the approximated set is 0.6 percentage points lower. Probation periods cannot be reconstructed for 2010–2015; a return to non-default is recognised after three consecutive month-ends without arrears above the threshold and without an FR&R case, which is recorded as data deficiency DD-LGDS-01 and covered by MoC component A1. From January 2016 to November 2020 the flag is reconstructed from daily data with the current definition, and from 1 December 2020 the production flag under CR-STD-110 v2.0 is used; the three definitions are analysed separately in Annex B, table B.4. The regulatory materiality threshold has been applied since 1 December 2020, the date of application set by De Nederlandsche Bank, and the RDS field DEF_FLAG_SOURCE identifies for every event which definition applies.

sections.heading: Default definition
sections.text: A default occurs when the obligor is more than 90 consecutive days past due on a material credit obligation or is considered unlikely to pay, in accordance with CRR Article 178 and CR-STD-110. Days past due are counted from the first day on which both the absolute component of EUR 100 and the relative component of 1% of the retail materiality threshold are exceeded, and counting restarts when either component is no longer exceeded. The absolute component is compared with the sum of all past due amounts of the obligor to the Bank and its subsidiaries, and the relative component divides that sum by the obligor's total on-balance-sheet exposure, excluding equity exposures. The relative threshold of 1% is the level set by De Nederlandsche Bank; no lower internal threshold is used as UTP indication. The obligor is defaulted when both components are exceeded for 90 consecutive days, with the default flag activated at the onset of the 91st day; for current account facilities, an overdrawn limit counts as past due from the first day of the excess. Days past due are computed daily in the SME arrears system (SAMS), and the date of default, the first day on which any criterion is met, is recorded for every event in DEF_DATE. Once the past due criterion is met the obligor is classified as defaulted without further judgement, unless a technical past due situation is confirmed.

sections.heading: Level of application, joint obligations and contagion
sections.text: Default is applied at obligor level for all retail SME exposures, consistent with the Bank's practice of managing SME clients as a single relationship; the level of application has not changed over the observation period. All credit obligations of a defaulted obligor, including private mortgages of a sole proprietor held by the Bank, are flagged as defaulted in all relevant systems. Partnerships (vof) and their partners are connected: the default of the partnership is propagated to the partners' exposures, as partners are jointly and severally liable, and joint obligations are treated as separate obligors in the materiality threshold calculation. Contagion within groups of connected clients (for example an operating company and its holding company) is specified in the connected clients procedure CC-PRC-02: default of an operating company leads to default of the holding when the holding's income depends on it for more than 50%; other cases are assessed individually by FR&R. The same definition of default is used by all Group entities with retail SME exposures in the Netherlands.

sections.heading: Counting of days past due
sections.text: Any amount of principal, interest or fee not paid when due, and any excess over the approved current account limit, is recognised as past due. Where the payment schedule has been modified, days past due are counted on the modified schedule, and each modification granted because of financial difficulties is assessed for distressed restructuring. Instalments deferred under the COVID-19 payment deferral scheme of 2020 were not counted as past due; the reasons for deferral were analysed, and 612 obligors were assessed as unlikely to pay. Counting is suspended for disputed amounts only where the dispute is before a court or Kifid. Technical past due is recognised only for errors of Bank systems, payment system failures and payment allocation time lags; each case is documented, corrected within 30 days and reviewed quarterly by Credit Risk Management. The policies on re-ageing, extensions, renewals of current account limits and netting of accounts are set in the SME arrears procedure SAMS-PRC-03 v2.4; renewal of an overdrawn limit without a credit decision is not permitted. The 640 technical past due events identified in the RDS are removed from the defaulted exposures used for estimation.

sections.heading: Return to non-defaulted status and multiple defaults
sections.text: An obligor returns to non-defaulted status only when no default trigger applies anymore, after a probation period of at least three months and an assessment by FR&R that the improvement is factual and permanent, based on recent financial statements and account behaviour. After a distressed restructuring, including WHOA restructuring plans, the probation period is at least 12 months from the latest of the restructuring, the default classification and the end of any grace period, and requires a material payment, no past due amounts and no doubt about full repayment. The probation start date and status are recorded for every default event. A facility that defaults again within 12 months of returning to non-defaulted status is treated as continuously defaulted from the first default; the period exceeds the nine months of EBA/GL/2017/16 paragraph 101 and is justified by the observation that 76% of SME re-defaults occur within 12 months. Default events are linked by DEF_CHAIN_ID; 1,560 events were merged into a preceding default, as listed in Annex B, table B.6, with all cash flows of both events included in the economic loss of the first.

sections.heading: Unlikeliness-to-pay triggers
sections.text: Non-accrued status, specific credit risk adjustments including IFRS 9 Stage 3, sale of a credit obligation at a credit-related loss above 5%, distressed restructuring with a diminished financial obligation above 1%, bankruptcy, suspension of payments or WSNP of the obligor, and the forced sale of collateral lead to default automatically. Facilities on which interest is no longer recognised because of a decline in credit quality are non-accrued and defaulted. Specific credit risk adjustments resulting from a significant decline in credit quality are UTP indications, collective Stage 1 and 2 allowances are not, and all Stage 3 exposures are defaulted. For every forbearance measure the diminished financial obligation (NPV0 - NPV1)/NPV0 is calculated at the original effective interest rate, and exposures above 1% are defaulted; forborne exposures below the threshold are assessed for a large final instalment, irregular schedules, grace periods and repeated forbearance, and all forborne non-performing exposures are defaulted. No SME credit obligations were sold in the observation period; a future sale would be assessed for the credit-related loss L = (E - P)/E against the threshold of 5%.

sections.heading: Additional indications and identification process
sections.text: Additional UTP indicators for SME exposures are a significant decline in turnover or cash flow, breach of financial covenants, negative equity in the annual accounts, tax arrears reported by the Tax Administration, fraud and a second forbearance request within 24 months; they lead to a case-by-case assessment by FR&R within 30 days of detection, whose outcome and rationale are recorded. External information used includes the Chamber of Commerce register, the Central Insolvency Register, BKR for sole proprietors, credit bureau alerts and sector news from Credit Risk Management's watch process. For each indication the identification method, information sources and monitoring frequency are defined in Annex A, table A.3, which maps each trigger to its source-system fields, and the operationalisation of each trigger is described in the SME default handbook DoD-HB-SME v1.8. Automatic triggers are identified daily by SAMS, manual triggers from watch lists, forbearance lists and specific provisions at least weekly, and all exposures of a defaulted obligor are flagged in all systems within one business day. Forborne non-performing exposures are verified monthly to be defaulted, and forborne performing exposures are reviewed quarterly for UTP indications. To ensure consistent labelling of judgement-based UTP flags, FR&R applies guideline UTP-GL-SME-01, and Credit Risk Management re-assesses a sample of 120 cases each year; agreement in 2026 was 95.8%.

sections.heading: Consistency of the default definition
sections.text: The same definition of default is used for the IRB approach, IFRS 9 Stage 3, non-performing exposure reporting and credit risk management, and forms the basis for SME credit monitoring and management reporting. The default triggers are implemented identically across SAMS, the SME lending platform and the Group's data warehouse, and completeness of default identification is reconciled monthly between SAMS and the default register. The RDS default flag is constructed in accordance with CR-STD-110 and is consistent with CRR Article 178; for 2021–2025 it matches the production default flag for 99.5% of events, the differences being explained by retroactive technical past due corrections. The IRB and IFRS 9 default flags are reconciled quarterly between the risk and finance systems. The register of default definitions maintained by Credit Risk Management records scope, approving body and date, implementation date, changes, change category and supervisory dates for every version. The prudential default flag and the accounting Stage 3 flag are labelled distinctly in the Group Data Catalogue.

sections.heading: Cure effectiveness and external data
sections.text: The effectiveness of the return-to-non-default policy is monitored annually: of SME obligors cured in 2022–2024, 13.8% re-defaulted within 12 months and 4.2% between 12 and 24 months, with the highest re-default rates after covenant-breach triggers. As a consequence, the probation period for covenant-breach defaults was extended to six months in CR-STD-110 v2.1 of 2025. No external or pooled default or loss data are used in the RDS. The rating system's scope contains a single definition of default for each period, so the estimation does not combine different default definitions within a period.

sections.heading: Data sources and lineage
sections.text: The RDS is built from the SME lending platform (BLP), the SME arrears system (SAMS), the workout system RECOV, the collateral management system (CMS, since June 2019; legacy system ZEKERHEDEN before), the BMKB guarantee administration and the general ledger. External inputs are the CBS house price index, the MSCI Netherlands commercial property capital value index received quarterly under licence, 3-month EURIBOR fixings and the RVO claim settlement statements for BMKB guarantees. Every RDS variable is traced from source table and field through the credit risk data warehouse to the RDS, with each transformation, filter, join and aggregation referenced to the build code module and the extraction frequency and timing, as documented in Annex A. For each type of risk data an authoritative source is defined (BLP for contract data, SAMS for arrears and defaults, RECOV for recoveries and costs, CMS for collateral, the BMKB administration for guarantees and the general ledger for write-offs). Two manual inputs exist, the mapping of ZEKERHEDEN collateral types to CMS collateral types and the sector mapping of legacy SBI codes, both version-controlled files whose lineage entries identify the four-eyes control applied. The lineage of the migrated collateral data was updated before use, when CMS replaced ZEKERHEDEN in 2019.

sections.heading: Data ownership and metadata
sections.text: The RDS draws on the data domains SME Lending, Credit Risk, Recovery and Collateral, each with exactly one Data Owner in the Group Data Catalogue, and the model data is mapped to these domains. Roles for data ownership and quality are defined for the business and for IT application owners. The model owner agreed data quality expectations for the critical data elements with the Data Owners in DQA-LGDS-2026 of 15 December 2026. Metadata for all RDS data elements are recorded and versioned in the Group Data Catalogue, using the Group identifiers for customers, facilities and collateral objects. Changes to definitions, sources or transformations are approved by the Data Owner and announced to the model owner in advance through the data change calendar. These arrangements implement the Bank's data governance under DATA-POL-001 for all model inputs.

sections.heading: Exclusions
sections.text: From 24,310 default events of facilities in the retail SME segment, 1,560 were merged into preceding defaults (section 3.3.3), leaving 22,750 events; the following exclusions, each approved by the model owner, were then applied. E1 technical past due: 640 events (2.8% of events; 0.6% of outstanding amount at default), removed because they are not defaults under CR-STD-110. E2 facilities outside the range of application at default: 412 events (1.8%; 6.9% of outstanding amount) of obligors whose group exposure exceeded EUR 1 million at default and which were therefore treated in the corporate rating system, whose LGD model covers them. No exclusion exceeds 5% of records in any segment; E2 exceeds 5% of the outstanding amount at default and was therefore approved by the model owner and reported to Model Validation on 18 February 2027. The conclusion of the impact analysis in section 5.3 is that E1 lowers and E2 has no material effect on the long-run average LGD. All other defaults observed in the observation period within the scope of the model are included in the LGD quantification.

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: Missing values are treated per variable as documented in Annex C, distinguishing values missing at random, for structural reasons and because of data deficiencies. The main case is the valuation date of collateral migrated from ZEKERHEDEN, missing for 11.2% of collateral objects of defaults before 2019 (data deficiency DD-LGDS-02); for these objects the date of the last credit review is used, which is conservative as it leads to a larger indexation adjustment. Sector code is missing for 0.9% of obligors (missing at random) and is set to the sector group 'other services'; imputations are reproducible in module impute_sme.py and the shares are reported in Annex C. Outliers are identified with documented criteria applied identically in development and production: collateral value above 20 times the exposure, time in default above 150 months and costs above 30% of the outstanding amount; collateral coverage is capped at 5 (212 facilities), which changes the LRA LGD by less than 0.01 percentage points. Missing values and outliers of the target variable and its constituents are not imputed; 94 records with missing cost booking dates were corrected at source.

sections.heading: Calculation of realised LGD
sections.text: Realised LGD is calculated per facility as economic loss divided by the outstanding amount at default, including principal, accrued interest and fees; economic loss equals the outstanding amount at default plus material direct and indirect costs, minus recoveries, with all cash flows after default discounted to the default date. Amounts forgiven before or at default are added to numerator and denominator; interest and fees capitalised before default are included in the outstanding amount, while amounts capitalised after default do not increase the economic loss. Additional drawings after default on current account facilities are included in the economic loss and not in the conversion factor, in line with CRM-STD-100 section 10.2, and therefore do not increase the outstanding amount at default in the denominator. Recoveries and costs booked in RECOV at obligor level are allocated to the obligor's facilities in proportion to the outstanding amount at default, except collateral proceeds, which are allocated to the facilities secured by that collateral according to the CMS allocation key. All recoveries, costs and additional drawings are discounted with the 3-month EURIBOR at the date of default plus 5 percentage points, the fixing being used as observed including negative values. For cured facilities an artificial cash flow equal to the outstanding amount at the date of return is included and discounted like observed cash flows; realised LGDs below zero are retained unfloored in the RDS.

sections.heading: Direct and indirect costs
sections.text: Direct costs comprise external legal fees, bankruptcy trustee fees, valuation and auction costs, and collection agency fees, booked per case in RECOV and reconciled to the general ledger. Indirect costs of FR&R and the SME arrears teams are allocated using the Bank's activity-based cost accounting: EUR 1,150 per cured case and EUR 4,820 per liquidation case at 2025 prices, indexed with the CPI. Pre-default collection costs are included for the months in arrears before default unless already in the outstanding amount. All material direct and indirect costs are stored per facility and month, and realised LGD therefore includes all material costs and additional drawings after default, as required by CRM-STD-100 section 9.2. The average realised LGD of cured facilities is 3.4%, reflecting costs and the discounting effect over an average time to cure of 11 months.

sections.heading: Reference dates in default
sections.text: For the ELBE and the LGD in-default, reference dates are defined at 0, 6, 12, 24, 36 and 48 months after default and at the date of the bankruptcy declaration, based on the recovery patterns of closed processes: most cures occur within 12 months, collateral sales between 6 and 30 months, and bankruptcy distributions after 36 months. At each reference date, realised LGD is calculated on the outstanding amount at that date, including fees and interest capitalised before it, with subsequent cash flows discounted to that date. The RDS stores for every defaulted facility the data used to assign it to an LGD pool in the year before default, the estimated LGD and the realised LGD. The RDS also stores for each reference date the outstanding amount, the time in default, the workout phase, the collateral values and the BMKB claim status.

sections.heading: Collateral data
sections.text: Collateral data are recorded in CMS with type, value, valuation date and method, lien or pledge rank and the allocation to secured facilities, meeting the data quality requirements of MRM-STD-022. Commercial real estate is valued by independent certified valuers at origination and revalued at least annually, residential property of entrepreneurs at least every three years with statistical indexation in between, and receivables and inventory through periodic pledge lists (monthly for limits above EUR 250,000, otherwise from the annual accounts). Immovable property is valued by qualified valuers independent of the credit decision, at or below market value, with the valuation reduced for prior-ranking claims. Equipment and vehicles are valued at market value, determined by independent appraisal for objects above EUR 250,000 and otherwise from book values adjusted with the appraisal-based ratio per object class. Collateral values used as drivers are taken at the reference date twelve months before default and at default, the earlier value being used where a revaluation shortly before default reflects credit deterioration. For second-ranking mortgages on the entrepreneur's private residence (37% of residential collateral) the prior-ranking claim is deducted, reflecting the subordinated position. Collateral not meeting CRR Article 181(1)(f), such as personal guarantees of directors, is not used as a driver; cash flows from it are recoveries without collateral, with their source recorded.

sections.heading: BMKB guarantee data
sections.text: For facilities guaranteed under the State's SME credit guarantee scheme (BMKB), administered by RVO, the RDS contains the guaranteed amount, the guarantee percentage, the claim date, the claim amount, the payment date and amount, and rejections with their reason. For partially guaranteed facilities, RVO payments and guarantee-related costs are allocated to the covered part, other cash flows and direct costs to the uncovered part, and indirect costs per EBA/GL/2017/16 paragraph 113, so that realised LGD of the uncovered part can be calculated. Between 2010 and 2025, 1,486 defaulted facilities carried a BMKB guarantee; RVO paid 91.2% of the claims by number (89.7% by amount), and rejections resulted mainly from late notification or use of funds outside the approved purpose. The ordering of recoveries (collateral proceeds, then BMKB claim, then unsecured collection) is recorded per case in RECOV, so that no protection is recognised twice.

sections.heading: Economic indicator data
sections.text: Economic indicators used for the downturn identification are stored with source, delivery date and version: GDP, unemployment and business bankruptcies from CBS, write-offs on loans to domestic non-financial SMEs from DNB statistics, gross value added per sector from CBS, and commercial property capital and rental value indices from MSCI. These official and licensed series are considered accurate and reliable; their revisions are tracked. As the exposures are located in the Netherlands, each indicator is included once at national level; sector value added is included for each sector group with more than 10% of EAD (construction, wholesale and retail trade, hospitality, business services, agriculture). Regional commercial property indices were considered but not acquired, as regional series start only in 2015 and the cost is disproportionate to their information value for the portfolio.

sections.heading: Representativeness
sections.text: Representativeness of the RDS for the current portfolio is assessed separately for risk differentiation (driver distributions) and risk quantification (loss levels), with the tests and thresholds of CRM-STD-100 section 6.5 and MV-HB-003 section 6. The analysis covers scope of application, definition of default, distribution of risk characteristics, lending standards and recovery policies, as detailed in Annex B. The scope of the RDS equals the range of application of version 2.0; the definition of default differs only for 2010–2015, for which the effect is quantified and covered by MoC. The RDS is representative of the current portfolio in risk drivers and loss levels, with the explained shifts reported in sections 5.1.1 and 5.1.2. The data used to develop the model are therefore representative, of adequate quality and sufficient in length and depth.

sections.heading: Representativeness of risk-driver distributions
sections.text: Driver distributions in the RDS, measured twelve months before default, were compared with the performing portfolio at 31 December 2025 using the PSI with ten buckets: collateral coverage 0.07, sector group 0.05, legal form 0.04, current account utilisation 0.11, arrears history 0.06, BMKB flag 0.02. The amber PSI for utilisation is explained by the lower average utilisation after 2021, when clients reduced their use of credit lines; the RDS covers the full range of utilisation with at least 900 defaults per bucket. As utilisation is a risk driver of the model and each range is represented, no bias results and no additional sample restriction or driver is needed. The share of other physical collateral located outside the Netherlands is 2.3% in the current portfolio and 1.9% in the RDS.

sections.heading: Representativeness of loss levels
sections.text: Loss levels were compared per calibration segment between the RDS and recent defaults: the realised LGD of closed processes of 2023–2025 defaults (26.1%) is close to the LRA (27.7%), and the two-sample tests of cure rates per segment show no significant difference. Comparability of the data for the long-run average was analysed for scope, default definition, risk characteristics, current and foreseeable economic conditions, and lending and recovery standards. Recovery-to-value ratios of commercial real estate in 2023–2025 (60.8%) are within the range observed over 2010–2025 (52%–66%).

sections.heading: Lending standards, recovery policies and legal environment
sections.text: Changes over the observation period were analysed by comparing RDS data before and after each change: the tightening of collateral requirements for business mortgages in 2014 (maximum LTV 80%), the centralisation of SME workout in FR&R in 2016, the migration to CMS in 2019 and the introduction of the WHOA in January 2021. After 2016, cure rates increased by 3.2 percentage points and time to recovery decreased by 4 months, which is reflected by the inclusion of these defaults in the estimates. WHOA restructurings (48 defaults since 2021) show lower recoveries for unsecured creditors than informal restructurings; the effect is not yet quantifiable with sufficient data and is covered by MoC component B1. Changes in the BMKB scheme, including the temporary BMKB-C variant of 2020–2021, are covered by MoC component B2.

sections.heading: Representativeness for other uses
sections.text: The LGD components are used for IFRS 9 ECL of the SME portfolio and in the SME pricing tool; both uses concern the same population as the RDS. For IFRS 9 the best estimate components without downturn adjustment, MoC and floors are used with forward-looking scenarios, as documented in chapter 1 of the MDD. The model is not used for corporate exposures or for exposures of other Group entities, which lie outside the range of application. Any use outside the RDS population would require a representativeness analysis before extension, as defined in the change procedure.

sections.heading: Impact of exclusions
sections.text: The effect of each exclusion on risk-driver distributions and realised LGD was quantified on the 22,750 events before exclusions. E1 (technical past due) has no effect on driver distributions (PSI 0.01) and would lower the LRA LGD by 0.2 percentage points if retained. E2 (obligors above EUR 1 million) concerns larger obligors with more real estate collateral; their inclusion would lower the LRA LGD by 0.4 percentage points, so the exclusion is conservative. The aggregate effect of all exclusions on the long-run average LGD is +0.6 percentage points (conservative) and was reported to Model Validation with the RDS.

sections.heading: Data quality assessment
sections.text: The data quality assessment of the RDS under MRM-STD-022 is reported in full in EVD-05-DQ; it was performed before estimation on RDS version LGDSME_RDS_v2027.1. All 47 RDS variables, including the 14 candidate risk drivers and the 21 data elements used to construct the target (default flag and date, outstanding amount, recoveries per source, costs, BMKB payments and write-offs), are critical data elements. Data quality was assessed on completeness, accuracy, consistency and timeliness, as well as validity, uniqueness and appropriateness, with 352 rules covering each applicable dimension per element. Thresholds follow MRM-STD-022 section 4.3, with stricter accuracy thresholds of 0.25% and 0.5% for the target constituents. Of the 352 rules, 338 are green, 14 amber and none red; the amber results concern the migrated collateral valuation dates, indirect costs before 2013 and the sector codes of legacy obligors. The assessment concluded that the RDS is fit for the intended use and was signed off by the model developer and the model owner on 19 February 2027, before the RDS was frozen.

sections.heading: Reconciliation, accuracy and controls
sections.text: Outstanding amounts at default were reconciled with BLP (difference 0.18%) and write-offs with the general ledger (0.26%); all default events were reconciled with the default register maintained under CR-STD-110. As MDL-05 is a Tier 2 model, reconciliation and automated rules are the primary accuracy checks; in addition, 150 collateral realisation files were verified against notarial and auction statements because of the collateral data migration. Controls operate from data entry to the RDS, including reconciliations across BLP, SAMS, RECOV, CMS and the general ledger, and the 352 rules are implemented in the Group DQ monitoring tool and applied monthly to the production input data of the LGD engine. Data are aggregated on a largely automated basis; the two manual mappings are documented and controlled. RDS data are reconcilable with accounting data and with COREP exposures of the same reference date. Critical data elements are reconciled with source and accounting data at least annually.

sections.heading: Completeness, consistency and timeliness
sections.text: Record-level completeness was confirmed against the default register and RECOV, and attribute-level completeness is 100% for 36 variables and above 88.8% for all others. Consistency is assessed between the RDS and the production input data, over the observation period including the three default definitions, and between related fields such as collateral sale date and proceeds. Timeliness is measured as the lag between reference date and availability and as the currency of collateral valuations; 4.1% of commercial real estate valuations in the current portfolio are older than the required annual refresh plus one month (amber). Where data are incomplete, the gaps are explained and their effect on the estimates assessed, in particular for the collateral data migrated in 2019. The data are sufficiently precise to avoid distortions of pool assignment and contain no known biases making them unfit for purpose. The DQ dashboard is reported monthly to the model owner and quarterly to the Credit Risk Management Committee.
