sections.heading: Data deficiencies
sections.text: Data deficiencies are recorded in the data deficiency log of MDL-05 with identifier, affected variables and segments, dimension, cause, impact and treatment, and each is linked to a margin of conservatism category. DD-LGDS-01: default flag approximated and probation not reconstructable for 2010–2015; impact −0.6 percentage points on LRA; MoC A1; limitations log L-02. DD-LGDS-02: valuation dates missing for 11.2% of migrated collateral objects of pre-2019 defaults and collateral types mapped from ZEKERHEDEN; conservative imputation and MoC A2; limitations log L-03. DD-LGDS-03: indirect costs before 2013 allocated with deflated 2013 unit costs; MoC assessed and included in A1 as the effect is below 0.05 percentage points; limitations log L-04. DD-LGDS-04: sector code missing for 0.9% of obligors; imputation, MoC assessed and rejected. Each deficiency not fully remediated is assessed for inclusion in the MoC as Category A, and the log references the MoC component. DD-LGDS-01 and -02 are permanent historical deficiencies reassessed annually; DD-LGDS-04 has a remediation owner (SME Lending data steward) and target date 30 September 2027, after which the related assessment is repeated.

sections.text: Deficiencies are remediated at source where feasible: 94 missing cost booking dates were corrected in RECOV, and 1,120 valuation dates were recovered from the archived valuation reports in 2026. No issue is rated high or critical, so no escalation to the Group Data Governance Committee or the Model Risk Committee was required. Deficiencies are identified systematically with the trigger list of CRM-STD-101 Annex 1 at every development, recalibration and annual review. Data quality of the model data is managed in accordance with MRM-STD-022.

sections.heading: Expert judgement in data treatment
sections.text: Expert judgement in data treatment is recorded in the expert judgement log EJ-LGDS of MDL-05, which is stored with the model documentation and referenced here and in chapter 11 of the MDD. EJ-LGDS-01 concerns the approximation of the default flag for 2010–2015 and EJ-LGDS-02 the mapping of ZEKERHEDEN collateral types to CMS types; the mapping file is the only manual input to the RDS build and is version controlled. EJ-LGDS-02 addresses data deficiency DD-LGDS-02 and is linked to MoC A2; its log entry records the rationale, the evidence (a comparison of 400 migrated objects with their original deeds), the rejected alternative of treating unmapped objects as unsecured, the impact (−0.3 percentage points on the other-secured LRA), the proposer, approver, approval date, review date and expiry condition. Both judgements are of medium materiality, were challenged by an independent senior modeller and approved by the model owner and the head of development; the proposer was not an approver. The rationale is specific enough to replicate the effect, as the mapping table and the approximation rule are implemented in versioned code.

sections.heading: Personal data and fair treatment
sections.text: The RDS contains personal data of natural persons, namely sole proprietors, partners and guarantors, processed for development, validation and application of the IRB model on the lawful basis of legal obligation (Article 6(1)(c) GDPR in conjunction with CRR Articles 144 and 179), recorded before processing started. The purposes are specified in the Record of Processing entry RoP-CR-0433, which is referenced in the model inventory record of MDL-05. sections.heading: Minimisation, pseudonymisation, retention and fair treatment
sections.text: Personal data attributes are limited to those needed: legal form, sector, account behaviour, collateral and guarantee data; names, addresses and dates of birth of natural persons are not included, and each attribute is justified in Annex A, table A.4 with purpose, lawful basis, pseudonymisation and retention period. Development and validation use pseudonymised data with keyed tokens held by the Data Custodian; re-identification requires Privacy Office approval and is logged, and the RDS is held in the secure analytics environment of Risk with role-based access. Test environments use masked data only, and personal data are kept accurate through the monthly refresh. The frozen RDS is retained for the period of use of the model plus five years, after which personal data are deleted or anonymised with evidence of deletion. No special categories of personal data are processed. Protected attributes (gender, nationality, age) of sole proprietors are excluded, and legal form and sector were screened as potential proxies; correlations with gender and age of sole proprietors are below 0.15, and the results are documented in Annex B, table B.9.

sections.heading: Reproducibility
sections.text: The RDS is built by versioned code in the repository rds-lgd-sme of the Bank's GitLab, tag v2.0.0, from source snapshots extracted on 15 January 2027, in Python 3.11.9 with pandas 2.2.2 and a locked dependency file. All extraction, transformation, exclusion, default flag construction and variable derivation steps are performed by build code without manual data manipulation. A full rebuild by a second developer on 22 February 2027 reproduced the frozen RDS exactly (21,698 default events, 1,412,300 cash-flow records and identical totals of discounted recoveries). The frozen RDS LGDSME_RDS_v2027.1 is stored read-only in the analytics environment, referenced in this document and in the MDD, and was signed off by the model owner on 22 February 2027 before estimation started. The RDS version is archived with its code, lineage and metadata, retained for the life of the model and ten years thereafter, and protected against alteration. Default, loss, recovery and exposure data are retained since 2010, beyond the observation periods required by the CRR. Data, code and documentation supporting the application for the material change remain available, and the RDS remains reproducible, throughout the ECB assessment.

sections.heading: Data dictionary and lineage
sections.text: The data dictionary lists all 47 RDS variables with business definition, source system and field, transformation, lineage and DQ rules. Each critical data element has a business definition, a technical definition and DQ rules per applicable dimension; for example COLL_VAL_DEF (collateral value at default: latest independent valuation indexed to the default date, net of prior-ranking claims; CMS.COLL_VALUE, CMS.PRIOR_CLAIM, MSCI or CBS index; rules on completeness, valuation age and non-negativity). Groups of variables: identifiers and dates (12), target constituents (21), candidate drivers (14: collateral coverage per type, BMKB coverage, legal form, sector group, relationship age, utilisation, arrears history, facility type, exposure size, region, lien rank, personal guarantee flag). Table A.3 maps every UTP trigger to its source field; table A.4 lists the personal data attributes with purpose, lawful basis, pseudonymisation and retention.

sections.heading: Representativeness analyses
sections.text: Annex B contains the detailed tables supporting chapter 5: B.1 defaults, closure and realised LGD per default year; B.2 PSI per driver and pool; B.3 cure rates and time in default per default year and segment; B.4 comparison of default definitions; B.5 before-and-after comparisons of policy changes; B.6 multiple defaults; B.7 exclusions; B.8 recoveries by source; B.9 proxy screening. Table B.3 shows the number of defaults returning to non-default within a fixed horizon of 24 months per default year, falling from 41.8% for 2010 defaults to 34.6% for 2013 defaults and rising to 45.9% for 2018 defaults. Table B.3 also shows time in default per default year, which increased from 22 months for 2010 defaults to 29 months for 2013 defaults. Table B.8 shows annual recoveries by source (real estate sales, other collateral realisation, BMKB claims, bankruptcy distributions and obligor payments), irrespective of default date and with and without repossessions, with recovery-to-value of commercial real estate falling to 52% in 2013. For incomplete processes, table B.8 shows marginal recoveries per year after default compared with those of complete processes of the same default year.

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: Annex C justifies the treatment of each variable with missing values or outliers and reports the affected shares. Collateral valuation date (migrated objects): 11.2% missing for pre-2019 defaults; date of last credit review used, on average 14 months earlier than the original valuation date where both are known, which increases the indexation adjustment and is conservative. Sector code: 0.9% missing at random; mapped to 'other services', whose realised LGD is close to the portfolio average. Relationship age: 2.4% missing for obligors migrated from the former SME brand, structural; set to the earliest facility start date. Collateral coverage: capped at 5 for 212 facilities; no outliers of the target are capped or excluded. All treatments are implemented in the build code and applied identically by the production engine, as confirmed in EVD-05-IMPL.

sections.heading: Purpose, scope and intended use
sections.text: This MDD describes the design, methodology, calibration, performance and limitations of version 2.0 of the LGD model for retail SME exposures (LGD-SME-RET, model identifier MDL-05), following the chapter structure, numbering and headings of the MDD template in MRM-STD-021 Annex B. The model produces the downturn LGD for performing exposures and the ELBE and LGD in-default for defaulted exposures of the retail SME portfolio, used for own funds requirements under the A-IRB approach; version 2.0 replaces version 1.4 once the ECB has granted permission for the material change. The MDD is detailed enough for Model Validation to understand the model and reproduce its estimation and calibration from the frozen RDS and the tagged code without recourse to the developers. Cover block: document version 0.9, status Draft, author K. Bos, reviewer A. Peeters; approval pending. The model is an internally developed quantitative method used for risk measurement, capital and pricing, managed under MRM-POL-001 and registered in the model inventory as MDL-05 since 2014.

sections.heading: Range of application and exposure class
sections.text: The range of application comprises retail exposures to SMEs and self-employed clients in the Netherlands whose group exposure does not exceed EUR 1 million: at 31 December 2026, 97,800 facilities of 61,200 obligors with an EAD of EUR 7.4 billion and an RWEA of EUR 3,386 million. Exposures are assigned to the retail exposure class (SME) by the exposure class module of the credit risk data warehouse, which checks monthly the EUR 1 million threshold at group level and the management of exposures on a pooled basis; obligors exceeding the threshold are transferred to the corporate rating system. Own LGD estimates are used only for these retail exposures; no exposures to institutions, financial sector entities or large corporates fall within the range of application. The IRB approach applies to all retail SME exposures of the Bank in the Netherlands; the roll-out plan for this class was completed in 2016 and was not used selectively. Retail SME exposures of the Belgian branch (EUR 84 million, 1.1% of the class) are under permanent partial use of the Standardised Approach as immaterial in size and risk profile, with quarterly triggers on number of obligors (1,000), EAD share (2%) and average risk weight, all currently met.

sections.heading: Intended use, users and use test
sections.text: Intended use is the calculation of own funds requirements; secondary uses are SME loan pricing, the SME credit risk appetite (expected loss, RWA density, NPE ratio), the internal capital allocation in the ICAAP, IFRS 9 ECL for SME and management reporting. The LGD determines the risk premium in the SME pricing tool, the collateral requirements in the credit approval of loans above EUR 250,000, the approval authority for facilities with an expected loss above 1%, and the limits of the SME risk appetite, and is reported quarterly to the Management Board. The IRB LGD is used in the internal capital allocation to the SME business line. Appetite metrics use parameters produced by this registered and approved model. LGD estimates for SME exposures have been used internally since 2010, more than three years before the IRB permission of 2014. For IFRS 9, the best estimate components without downturn, MoC and floors are used; the removal of the MoC is documented and reasonable because IFRS 9 requires unbiased estimates. Limitations and conditions are communicated to users through the user note LGD-SME-UN-2027 and the limitations log in chapter 8.

sections.heading: Tier, inventory and classification
sections.text: The model is Tier 2: materiality Medium (EAD EUR 7.4 billion, 6.4% of credit RWEA) and complexity Medium, mapped to Tier 2 by the matrix of MRM-STD-010 section 6.4, which is the minimum tier for a model used for own funds requirements. The tier was proposed with the tiering template, approved by MRM and confirmed at validation; it was reviewed for the material change on 3 May 2027 without change and is not lower than the matrix outcome. The inventory names the model owner (Head of SME Credit Risk Modelling), the developer (SME Credit Risk Modelling), the main users and the validation team (Model Validation – Credit Risk), and records the lifecycle stage (Change – material change application), the latest validation opinion of version 1.4, open findings, conditions, limitations and the post-model adjustment. It records the supervisory permission status (permission of 2014, material change of 2016) and the open supervisory obligation O-2 of the ECB decision of 12 December 2024 on the downturn LGD, with owner and deadline. The model owner updates the record within ten business days of any change and attests it quarterly; all mandatory attributes are complete. Since gate G1 the inventory records that the model is not an AI system under the AI Act, being a statistical model with fixed logic that does not adapt after deployment; the complexity assessment classifies it as medium and not highly complex or dynamic. The rating system is classified as material and communicated as such to the ECB.

sections.heading: Model design
sections.text: For a performing facility, LGD = P(cure) x LGC + (1 − P(cure)) x LGL; the loss given liquidation is LGL = [E_U x LGL_U + sum over collateral types of costs − BMKB recovery] / EAD, where the secured part E_S = min(EAD, sum of V_c x (1 − h_c)) is covered by collateral value V_c after the haircut h_c, and E_U = EAD − E_S is the unsecured part. P(cure) is estimated by logistic regression, haircuts per collateral type from realised recovery-to-value ratios of closed liquidations, LGL_U by segment averages of realised unsecured recoveries, and the BMKB recovery from the guaranteed amount, the observed claim acceptance rate and the average payment lag. The structure reflects the SME workout process, in which a default ends with a cure after restructuring, or with the realisation of collateral, a BMKB claim and a bankruptcy distribution on the unsecured part. Facility-level estimates are used for risk differentiation; risk quantification is performed at the level of 10 LGD pools in three calibration segments. The design and operational details of the rating system, the rationale for the rating criteria and the major changes from version 1.4 are documented in this MDD, evidencing compliance with the IRB requirements.

sections.heading: Segmentation, pools and assignment
sections.text: Three calibration segments with significantly different loss profiles are defined by the dominant collateral: real estate secured (58% of EAD), other secured (19%) and unsecured (23%); sector groups and regions were tested and showed no significantly different loss profiles after collateral coverage, and all exposures are in the Netherlands. Facilities are assigned to 10 LGD pools (LS01–LS04 real estate, LS05–LS07 other secured, LS08–LS10 unsecured) by the facility-level LGD score with fixed boundaries, applied identically across regions, channels and business teams. Assignment considers obligor characteristics (legal form, sector group, arrears history, utilisation) and transaction characteristics (collateral types and coverage, BMKB guarantee, facility type). Each pool holds at least 486 RDS defaults and 5,200 current facilities, and no pool exceeds 22% of EAD. Pool assignment is automated in RCE and updated monthly with current collateral values, utilisation and arrears; missing collateral values lead to treatment as unsecured, the most conservative assignment. Coefficients, haircuts, pool boundaries and pool LGDs in tables 4.2, 4.3 and 5.8 allow third parties to replicate the assignment. The model depends on the retail SME PD model MDL-04 through the shared default flag, and on the CCF model for SME current accounts for EAD.

sections.heading: Data
sections.text: The model is estimated on the approved RDS documented in EVD-05-RDS v1.0, frozen as LGDSME_RDS_v2027.1 (21,698 defaults of 2010–2025, cash flows to 31 December 2026). The same defaults and definition of default underlie the performing LGD, ELBE and LGD in-default. Samples were defined before estimation: defaults of 2010–2022 were split randomly (seed 20270301, stratified by year and segment) into development (13,832) and out-of-sample (3,458) samples, and defaults of 2023–2025 (4,408) form the out-of-time sample, not used for variable selection or estimation. The final calibration of the pool LGDs uses all 21,698 defaults. RDS deficiencies DD-LGDS-01 to -04 are cross-referenced to the limitations log and the MoC components.

sections.heading: Methodological alternatives
sections.text: Three alternatives were assessed against regulatory compliance, data needs, performance, stability, interpretability and implementation: (A) the version 1.4 approach of pool-level LRA without collateral components, (B) the component model with collateral haircuts and BMKB recovery, and (C) a direct fractional regression of realised LGD with collateral coverage as driver. On the out-of-time sample, the gAUC is 0.611 for A, 0.648 for B and 0.639 for C. Alternative B was selected because it performs best, recognises the collateral types in line with the recovery process, allows downturn haircuts to be applied per collateral type and is transparent to credit officers; alternative C mixes the collateral types into a single driver and cannot reflect the BMKB guarantee explicitly. The design is conceptually sound and consistent with the economics of SME losses, driven by the probability of restructuring and by collateral and guarantee recoveries.

sections.heading: Variable selection and cure component
sections.text: The long list of 14 candidate drivers combined statistical analysis with input from FR&R, SME credit risk management and literature, and each candidate was assessed for economic rationale, availability in RCE and stability, with the expected sign stated in the development plan. Univariate screening, stepwise selection at the 1% level and resolution of correlations above 0.6 (utilisation retained over overdraft days) led to the final drivers, all with expected sign and plausible magnitude. P(cure) coefficients (table 4.2): intercept 0.412; private limited company +0.284; sector hospitality −0.331; sector construction −0.296; arrears in preceding 12 months −0.574; utilisation above 90% −0.418; relationship age above 10 years +0.197; all significant at the 1% level. The AUC of P(cure) is 0.702 on the development, 0.694 on the out-of-sample and 0.681 on the out-of-time sample. The rationale and analyses supporting the choice of rating criteria are documented in Annex 2.

sections.heading: Collateral haircuts
sections.text: Haircuts are estimated per collateral type as one minus the default-weighted average recovery-to-value of closed liquidations, where recoveries are net of sale costs and discounted to default: commercial real estate 38%, residential real estate 24%, receivables 62%, inventory 79%, equipment and vehicles 68% (long-run average). The haircuts reflect that recoveries fall short of market value because of forced-sale discounts, time to realisation, costs and the risk that the Bank cannot gain control of the collateral, notably inventory and vehicles that the obligor may sell or move. Inventory and equipment on the obligor's premises are subject to the ground privilege of the Tax Administration under Article 22 of the Collection of State Taxes Act 1990, which ranks ahead of the non-possessory pledge; this is reflected in the haircuts, which are estimated on recoveries after the Tax Administration's claims. Potential decreases in collateral value until realisation are reflected through the downturn haircuts; no adjustment is made for potential increases in value. The haircut for inventory is based on 212 closed cases and was set by expert panel (EJ-LGDS-03) at 79% against a statistical estimate of 74%. Only collateral meeting CRR Article 181(1)(f) is recognised; no liability of the obligor is recognised as collateral, and the dependence between the obligor's business and collateral such as inventory and receivables is addressed by estimating haircuts on defaulted obligors only.

sections.heading: Legal enforceability of collateral
sections.text: Mortgages on real estate, including the right of summary execution under Article 3:268 of the Dutch Civil Code, disclosed and undisclosed pledges on receivables and non-possessory pledges on inventory and equipment are enforceable under Dutch law, as confirmed by the written legal opinion of independent external counsel of 22 September 2026, which also covers enforceability in bankruptcy of the obligor. The opinion was renewed for version 2.0 because receivables, inventory and equipment are newly recognised, and a new opinion will be obtained for any substantive change of the pledge documentation. The opinion addresses the governing law and the jurisdiction of realisation, which is the Netherlands for 97.7% of other physical collateral. No funded protection is recognised in the exposure value through netting, so no double recognition arises.

sections.heading: Recognition of the BMKB guarantee
sections.text: The BMKB guarantee of the State of the Netherlands, administered by RVO, is recognised through the modelling approach: the BMKB recovery is a component of LGL based on the guaranteed amount, the claim acceptance rate (89.7% by amount) and the payment lag (7 months on average after the claim); PD is not adjusted. The criteria for recognition address the guarantor's ability and willingness to pay, the timing of payment, the absence of correlation between the State and the obligor, and the residual risk from rejections; there is no currency mismatch and the guarantor is not in default. Enforceability of the BMKB terms was confirmed by a written legal opinion of independent counsel, to be renewed for substantive changes of the scheme. Personal guarantees of directors are ineligible and their cash flows are treated as unprotected recoveries with source recorded; credit insurance is not used. Recoveries are allocated in the order collateral, BMKB, unsecured collection, so that no protection is recognised twice, and the final risk weight of BMKB-guaranteed exposures is not lower than that of a comparable direct exposure to the guarantor. For partially guaranteed facilities, RVO payments and guarantee costs are allocated to the covered part as described in section 4.5.1 of the RDS documentation.

sections.heading: Incomplete workouts and maximum recovery period
sections.text: Future recoveries of the 1,828 incomplete processes are estimated from the recovery patterns of closed processes with the same time in default, segment and workout phase, using the 25th percentile pattern for bankruptcy cases; back-testing on processes closed in 2025–2026 shows estimated recoveries of 96.4% of realised recoveries, and the residual uncertainty is covered by MoC A3. Incomplete processes enter the LRA with these estimated recoveries, so LGD is based on all defaults in the RDS. The maximum recovery period of 72 months (EJ-LGDS-04) is supported by the observed pace of recoveries and consistent with bankruptcy proceedings in the Netherlands.

sections.heading: Calibration
sections.text: The long-run average LGD of each pool is the default-weighted arithmetic average of realised LGDs of all RDS defaults in the pool, including estimated future recoveries; yearly averages are not used. Realised LGDs reflecting a profit are set to zero for observed and long-run average LGD, while unfloored values are used in the haircut estimation. The LRA LGD is 27.7% overall: 15.2% for real estate secured, 31.8% for other secured and 44.6% for unsecured facilities; calibration is tested at pool and segment level, and no pool shows significant underestimation. Estimates rely on the Bank's own loss experience and not on market prices, and are representative of long-run experience including the 2012–2014 downturn.

sections.heading: Identification of the economic downturn
sections.text: The economic downturn for the type of exposures 'retail SME' was identified in January 2027 under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/930, separately from other types of exposures. The relevant indicator set comprises GDP, the unemployment rate, CBS business bankruptcies as external default rate, DNB write-offs on SME loans as external credit loss, value added of the five material sector groups, the MSCI commercial property capital value and rental value indices, and the CBS house price index for residential collateral of entrepreneurs. Sector value added is included separately per material sector group, because the sectors did not co-move strongly (hospitality and construction reached their troughs in different years), so a common indicator is not used. GDP, value added and property indices are analysed in 12-month changes, unemployment in levels, and bankruptcies and write-offs in 12-month sums. For each indicator the most severe 12-month value over the 20 years ending December 2025 was determined, considering periods starting in any month; the span was assessed as representative because it includes the 2009 recession, the 2013 bankruptcy peak and the 2020 pandemic shock, and was not extended.

sections.heading: Downturn periods
sections.text: Most severe values: GDP −9.1% and hospitality value added −38.6% (12 months to June 2020); construction value added −10.2% (12 months to June 2010); unemployment 7.5% (to February 2014); bankruptcies, SME write-offs, retail trade value added and commercial property capital (−8.9%) and rental values (to December 2013 and March 2014). The correlated indicators peaking in 2013–2014 are merged into one downturn period DP-B from April 2012 to March 2014, which covers all related peaks and is extended because bankruptcies remained within 10% of their peak throughout 2013. GDP and hospitality form DP-A (July 2019–June 2020), and construction forms DP-C (July 2009–June 2010), each equal to the 12-month period of the most severe value. The periods are based on observed conditions, not on stress scenarios, reflect cyclical effects and are reviewed annually and when new information arises.

sections.heading: Downturn impact analysis and quantification
sections.text: For DP-B the impact analysis shows realised LGD per default year rising from 25.1% (2010) to 31.4% (2012) and 32.8% (2013), cure rates within 24 months falling to 34.6%, time in default rising to 29 months and recovery-to-value of commercial real estate falling to 52%, with a lag of up to 12 months, so that defaults up to March 2015 are attributed to DP-B. For DP-A no impact is observed because of support measures; for DP-C, which precedes the RDS, loss data are insufficient, and the downturn LGD is estimated with an extrapolation approach based on the statistically significant dependency between construction-sector LGL and construction value added (slope 0.84, p < 0.01), with a strictly positive Category A MoC from the 90% confidence interval. For DP-B the components are recalibrated on the defaults of the period, starting with the haircuts, which show the highest impact (downturn haircuts: commercial real estate 46%, residential 31%, receivables 66%, inventory 83%, equipment 72%), then LGL_U and P(cure); recalibration on the same cohort preserves their dependency, and cash flows after 72 months are excluded. Applied to the current portfolio including final MoC, the average downturn LGD is 29.8% for DP-A, 35.0% for DP-B and 31.1% for DP-C; DP-B is selected for all segments, with downturn best estimates of 20.1% (real estate), 37.0% (other secured) and 50.2% (unsecured). Downturn LGD is calibrated at pool level and aggregated to segment level, and the downturn LGD plus MoC exceeds the LRA plus MoC in all segments, so the downturn estimate is used, in accordance with EBA/GL/2019/03 and the requirements of EBA/GL/2017/16, and documented per segment in table 5.3.

sections.heading: ELBE, LGD in-default and floors
sections.text: An ELBE and LGD in-default are assigned to every defaulted exposure, estimated per reference date in default (0, 6, 12, 24, 36, 48 months and bankruptcy declaration) from realised LGDs at that reference date. The ELBE contains no MoC and reflects current circumstances through the current collateral values and workout phase; the LGD in-default adds a downturn component, inferred from the DP-B calibration per reference date, and the MoC. LGD in-default exceeds the ELBE for all exposures and is raised where the specific credit risk adjustment exceeds it; at 31 December 2026 the ELBE averages 38.2% and the LGD in-default 43.9% for 1,940 defaulted facilities (add-on: 3.6 pp downturn, 2.1 pp MoC). The final performing LGD is floored at exposure level after downturn adjustment and MoC with the input floors of CRR Article 164(4): 30% for the unsecured part and 10% for receivables and immovable property and 15% for other physical collateral on the secured part, combined as in Article 161(6); the floor binds for 9.7% of EAD. The order best estimate, downturn, MoC, floor is identical in development and RCE.

sections.heading: Margin of conservatism
sections.text: The final LGD is the best estimate including appropriate adjustments plus a MoC quantified under CRM-STD-101 in Categories A, B and C. Deficiencies were identified with the trigger list of CRM-STD-101 Annex 1, including those considered and rejected (DD-LGDS-04), and an appropriate adjustment was considered first for each. Each deficiency is linked to one category and recorded in the MoC register with identifier, affected segments and reference to the data deficiency log; deficiencies found by validation, monitoring, audit or supervision are added within three months. A1 default flag approximation: +0.4 pp in all segments (60-dpd alternative); A2 migrated collateral data: +0.5, +0.8 and 0.0 pp (range of valuation-date alternatives); A3 incomplete workouts: +0.4, +0.6, +0.5 pp; B1 WHOA: +0.3, +0.4, +0.5 pp; B2 BMKB scheme changes: +0.1, +0.1, +0.2 pp. Each deficiency is quantified per segment before aggregation, is non-negative and not lower than the adverse sensitivity result, and favourable effects do not offset other components; no expert judgement was needed for quantification.

sections.heading: Discriminatory power, calibration and stability
sections.text: The gAUC is 0.664 on development, 0.659 out-of-sample and 0.648 out-of-time (relative decrease 2.4%), against 0.611 for version 1.4 on the same out-of-time sample; per segment it ranges from 0.611 to 0.672. The model differentiates risk adequately, with drivers forming a reasonable basis and no material bias. On the out-of-time sample, realised LGD of closed cases (24.9%) is below the best estimate (26.3%), and the one-sided paired t-test shows no underestimation in any pool; back-testing is done at component and facility level. Kruskal–Wallis and Mann–Whitney tests confirm homogeneity within and heterogeneity between adjacent pools; pools were merged where not distinct (EJ-LGDS-05). Coefficients re-estimated on 2010–2017 and 2018–2025 defaults are consistent within two standard errors.

sections.heading: Benchmarking and sensitivity
sections.text: As a Tier 2 model, version 2.0 was compared with version 1.4 as benchmark: gAUC 0.648 against 0.611, and final EAD-weighted LGD 30.4% against 31.8% (including the post-model adjustment), the difference being explained by the recognition of receivables, inventory and equipment and the new downturn calibration. In the 2026 supervisory benchmarking under CRD Article 78, the Bank submitted retail SME LGD results with methodology explanations; the Bank's average LGD of 31.8% compared with an EU median of 33.5%. Sensitivity analyses covered maximum recovery period (60 and 84 months: −0.3 and +0.1 pp), discount add-on ±1 pp (±0.6 pp), inventory haircut 74% and 84% (−0.2 and +0.2 pp), calibration window 2013–2025 (−0.5 pp) and the alternative default flag approximations; results support the MoC quantification. The amber PSI of utilisation was analysed and recorded in the limitations log as L-06.

sections.heading: Assumptions and limitations
sections.text: Material assumptions: recovery patterns of closed processes apply to incomplete ones; haircuts observed in 2010–2025 remain valid; the BMKB scheme continues; collateral valuations at origination and indexation represent realisable value; the model is used only within its range of application. The model does not work effectively for exposures above EUR 1 million, for collateral located outside the Netherlands, for sectors newly entered by the Bank, or under a WHOA-dominated recovery environment not represented in the RDS. The limitations log (chapter 8.1 of this MDD) states for each entry identifier, description, source, impact, mitigant and owner: L-01 incomplete workouts (MoC A3), L-02 default flag approximation (MoC A1), L-03 migrated collateral data (MoC A2), L-04 indirect costs before 2013, L-05 inventory haircut based on few observations (EJ-LGDS-03), L-06 utilisation shift, L-07 WHOA experience (MoC B1). The log is kept up to date, material limitations are reported to the approval authority at G3 and recorded in the inventory, and they are communicated to users. Approximations used in risk reports based on model outputs are documented here and supported by the back-testing.

sections.heading: Monitoring
sections.text: The monitoring plan, approved by the model owner and reviewed by Model Validation, defines KPIs, calculation, thresholds, frequency, periods, segments, responsibilities and escalation. KPIs: back-testing of realised versus estimated LGD (one-sided t-test, amber p < 5%, red p < 1%; portfolio underestimation above 5% relative amber and 10% red), gAUC decrease (amber above 10%, red above 20%), PSI of pools and drivers (amber 0.10, red 0.25), realised versus predicted cure rates, recovery-to-value per collateral type, BMKB acceptance rate, ELBE back-test, production DQ, overrides and coverage. KPIs are computed for the model, each segment and each pool, semi-annually as required for Tier 2, and reported within 60 days; the plan is updated with every change and reviewed annually. Amber results are analysed and documented; red results or repeated amber are notified to MRM and Model Validation within ten business days with a root cause analysis and action plan within 60 days, proposing no action, overlay, recalibration, redevelopment or restriction, and unresolved triggers after six months go to the MRC. The review-of-estimates framework defines scope, frequency, metrics, thresholds and actions, reviews estimates at least annually, and revises estimates upward where realised values continue to exceed estimates, with a recalibration plan approved by the MRC within three months after a red outcome. The annual review covers representativeness, performance on the whole application portfolio and back-testing per pool, concludes on fitness for purpose, and is provided to Model Validation; monitoring code is versioned in lgd-sme-monitoring.

sections.heading: Expert judgement and overrides
sections.text: Every expert judgement is recorded in the log EJ-LGDS, referenced here, and approved before use: EJ-LGDS-01 default flag approximation (medium), EJ-LGDS-02 collateral type mapping (medium), EJ-LGDS-03 inventory haircut (medium, +0.2 pp), EJ-LGDS-04 maximum recovery period of 72 months (low), EJ-LGDS-05 pool merges (low). Each entry records type, stage, affected parameter, rationale, evidence and alternatives, quantified impact, proposer, approver, dates and expiry conditions, and design judgements are justified in the relevant sections of this MDD. EJ-LGDS-03 was elicited from a panel of five FR&R workout specialists in two Delphi rounds; the panel composition and method are documented, and the aggregate result was set at the median. Medium judgements were independently challenged and approved by the model owner and head of development; the aggregate effect is +0.6 pp (2.0% relative), below the high threshold, and the effect of judgement on performance is negligible. Pool assignment of performing exposures cannot be overridden; FR&R may override collateral values of defaulted exposures only for a closed list of reasons (signed sale agreement, new valuation, confirmed fraud), with the evidence value as maximum and approval by a senior credit officer independent of the case handler, stricter for favourable overrides. Each override is recorded with reason code, rationale, evidence, proposer and approver; override rates (3.4% of defaulted facilities in 2026) are monitored semi-annually and overridden cases analysed annually against pre-override values, including per approving officer. Human oversight by FR&R and credit risk management complements the model and detects errors from model weaknesses.

sections.heading: Purpose, scope and intended use
sections.text: This MDD describes the design, methodology, calibration, performance and limitations of version 2.0 of the LGD model for retail SME exposures (LGD-SME-RET, model identifier MDL-05), following the chapter structure, numbering and headings of the MDD template in MRM-STD-021 Annex B. The model produces the downturn LGD for performing exposures and the ELBE and LGD in-default for defaulted exposures of the retail SME portfolio, used for own funds requirements under the A-IRB approach; version 2.0 replaces version 1.4 once the ECB has granted permission for the material change. The MDD is detailed enough for Model Validation to understand the model and reproduce its estimation and calibration from the frozen RDS and the tagged code without recourse to the developers. Cover block: document version 1.0, status Approved, author K. Bos, reviewer A. Peeters, approvers M. Mulder (model owner) and R. Kuipers (Head of Credit Risk Modelling), approval date 7 May 2027. The model is an internally developed quantitative method used for risk measurement, capital and pricing, managed under MRM-POL-001 and registered in the model inventory as MDL-05 since 2014.

sections.heading: Range of application and exposure class
sections.text: The range of application comprises retail exposures to SMEs and self-employed clients in the Netherlands whose group exposure does not exceed EUR 1 million: at 31 December 2026, 97,800 facilities of 61,200 obligors with an EAD of EUR 7.4 billion and an RWEA of EUR 3,386 million. Exposures are assigned to the retail exposure class (SME) by the exposure class module of the credit risk data warehouse, which checks monthly the EUR 1 million threshold at group level and the management of exposures on a pooled basis; obligors exceeding the threshold are transferred to the corporate rating system. Own LGD estimates are used only for these retail exposures; no exposures to institutions, financial sector entities or large corporates fall within the range of application. The IRB approach applies to all retail SME exposures of the Bank in the Netherlands; the roll-out plan for this class was completed in 2016 and was not used selectively. Retail SME exposures of the Belgian branch (EUR 84 million, 1.1% of the class) are under permanent partial use of the Standardised Approach as immaterial in size and risk profile, with quarterly triggers on number of obligors (1,000), EAD share (2%) and average risk weight, all currently met.

sections.heading: Intended use, users and use test
sections.text: Intended use is the calculation of own funds requirements; secondary uses are SME loan pricing, the SME credit risk appetite (expected loss, RWA density, NPE ratio), the internal capital allocation in the ICAAP, IFRS 9 ECL for SME and management reporting. The LGD determines the risk premium in the SME pricing tool, the collateral requirements in the credit approval of loans above EUR 250,000, the approval authority for facilities with an expected loss above 1%, and the limits of the SME risk appetite, and is reported quarterly to the Management Board. The IRB LGD is used in the internal capital allocation to the SME business line. Appetite metrics use parameters produced by this registered and approved model. LGD estimates for SME exposures have been used internally since 2010, more than three years before the IRB permission of 2014. For IFRS 9, the best estimate components without downturn, MoC and floors are used; the removal of the MoC is documented and reasonable because IFRS 9 requires unbiased estimates. Limitations and conditions are communicated to users through the user note LGD-SME-UN-2027 and the limitations log in chapter 8.

sections.heading: Model design
sections.text: For a performing facility, LGD = P(cure) x LGC + (1 − P(cure)) x LGL; the loss given liquidation is LGL = [E_U x LGL_U + sum over collateral types of costs − BMKB recovery] / EAD, where the secured part E_S = min(EAD, sum of V_c x (1 − h_c)) is covered by collateral value V_c after the haircut h_c, and E_U = EAD − E_S is the unsecured part. P(cure) is estimated by logistic regression, haircuts per collateral type from realised recovery-to-value ratios of closed liquidations, LGL_U by segment averages of realised unsecured recoveries, and the BMKB recovery from the guaranteed amount, the observed claim acceptance rate and the average payment lag. The structure reflects the SME workout process, in which a default ends with a cure after restructuring, or with the realisation of collateral, a BMKB claim and a bankruptcy distribution on the unsecured part. Facility-level estimates are used for risk differentiation; risk quantification is performed at the level of 10 LGD pools in three calibration segments. The design and operational details of the rating system, the rationale for the rating criteria and the major changes from version 1.4 are documented in this MDD, evidencing compliance with the IRB requirements.

sections.heading: Segmentation, pools and assignment
sections.text: Three calibration segments with significantly different loss profiles are defined by the dominant collateral: real estate secured (58% of EAD), other secured (19%) and unsecured (23%); sector groups and regions were tested and showed no significantly different loss profiles after collateral coverage, and all exposures are in the Netherlands. Facilities are assigned to 10 LGD pools (LS01–LS04 real estate, LS05–LS07 other secured, LS08–LS10 unsecured) by the facility-level LGD score with fixed boundaries, applied identically across regions, channels and business teams. Assignment considers obligor characteristics (legal form, sector group, arrears history, utilisation) and transaction characteristics (collateral types and coverage, BMKB guarantee, facility type). Each pool holds at least 486 RDS defaults and 5,200 current facilities, and no pool exceeds 22% of EAD. Pool assignment is automated in RCE and updated monthly with current collateral values, utilisation and arrears; missing collateral values lead to treatment as unsecured, the most conservative assignment. Coefficients, haircuts, pool boundaries and pool LGDs in tables 4.2, 4.3 and 5.8 allow third parties to replicate the assignment. The model depends on the retail SME PD model MDL-04 through the shared default flag, and on the CCF model for SME current accounts for EAD.

sections.heading: Methodological alternatives
sections.text: Three alternatives were assessed against regulatory compliance, data needs, performance, stability, interpretability and implementation: (A) the version 1.4 approach of pool-level LRA without collateral components, (B) the component model with collateral haircuts and BMKB recovery, and (C) a direct fractional regression of realised LGD with collateral coverage as driver. On the out-of-time sample, the gAUC is 0.611 for A, 0.648 for B and 0.639 for C. Alternative B was selected because it performs best, recognises the collateral types in line with the recovery process, allows downturn haircuts to be applied per collateral type and is transparent to credit officers; alternative C mixes the collateral types into a single driver and cannot reflect the BMKB guarantee explicitly. The design is conceptually sound and consistent with the economics of SME losses, driven by the probability of restructuring and by collateral and guarantee recoveries.

sections.heading: Variable selection and cure component
sections.text: The long list of 14 candidate drivers combined statistical analysis with input from FR&R, SME credit risk management and literature, and each candidate was assessed for economic rationale, availability in RCE and stability, with the expected sign stated in the development plan. Univariate screening, stepwise selection at the 1% level and resolution of correlations above 0.6 (utilisation retained over overdraft days) led to the final drivers, all with expected sign and plausible magnitude. P(cure) coefficients (table 4.2): intercept 0.412; private limited company +0.284; sector hospitality −0.331; sector construction −0.296; arrears in preceding 12 months −0.574; utilisation above 90% −0.418; relationship age above 10 years +0.197; all significant at the 1% level. The AUC of P(cure) is 0.702 on the development, 0.694 on the out-of-sample and 0.681 on the out-of-time sample. The rationale and analyses supporting the choice of rating criteria are documented in Annex 2.

sections.heading: Collateral haircuts
sections.text: Haircuts are estimated per collateral type as one minus the default-weighted average recovery-to-value of closed liquidations, where recoveries are net of sale costs and discounted to default: commercial real estate 38%, residential real estate 24%, receivables 62%, inventory 79%, equipment and vehicles 68% (long-run average). The haircuts reflect that recoveries fall short of market value because of forced-sale discounts, time to realisation, costs and the risk that the Bank cannot gain control of the collateral, notably inventory and vehicles that the obligor may sell or move. Inventory and equipment on the obligor's premises are subject to the ground privilege of the Tax Administration under Article 22 of the Collection of State Taxes Act 1990, which ranks ahead of the non-possessory pledge; this is reflected in the haircuts, which are estimated on recoveries after the Tax Administration's claims. Potential decreases in collateral value until realisation are reflected through the downturn haircuts; no adjustment is made for potential increases in value. The haircut for inventory is based on 212 closed cases and was set by expert panel (EJ-LGDS-03) at 79% against a statistical estimate of 74%. Only collateral meeting CRR Article 181(1)(f) is recognised; no liability of the obligor is recognised as collateral, and the dependence between the obligor's business and collateral such as inventory and receivables is addressed by estimating haircuts on defaulted obligors only.

sections.heading: Legal enforceability of collateral
sections.text: Mortgages on real estate, including the right of summary execution under Article 3:268 of the Dutch Civil Code, disclosed and undisclosed pledges on receivables and non-possessory pledges on inventory and equipment are enforceable under Dutch law, as confirmed by the written legal opinion of independent external counsel of 22 September 2026, which also covers enforceability in bankruptcy of the obligor. The opinion was renewed for version 2.0 because receivables, inventory and equipment are newly recognised, and a new opinion will be obtained for any substantive change of the pledge documentation. The opinion addresses the governing law and the jurisdiction of realisation, which is the Netherlands for 97.7% of other physical collateral. No funded protection is recognised in the exposure value through netting, so no double recognition arises.

sections.heading: Recognition of the BMKB guarantee
sections.text: The BMKB guarantee of the State of the Netherlands, administered by RVO, is recognised through the modelling approach: the BMKB recovery is a component of LGL based on the guaranteed amount, the claim acceptance rate (89.7% by amount) and the payment lag (7 months on average after the claim); PD is not adjusted. The criteria for recognition address the guarantor's ability and willingness to pay, the timing of payment, the absence of correlation between the State and the obligor, and the residual risk from rejections; there is no currency mismatch and the guarantor is not in default. Enforceability of the BMKB terms was confirmed by a written legal opinion of independent counsel, to be renewed for substantive changes of the scheme. Personal guarantees of directors are ineligible and their cash flows are treated as unprotected recoveries with source recorded; credit insurance is not used. Recoveries are allocated in the order collateral, BMKB, unsecured collection, so that no protection is recognised twice, and the final risk weight of BMKB-guaranteed exposures is not lower than that of a comparable direct exposure to the guarantor. For partially guaranteed facilities, RVO payments and guarantee costs are allocated to the covered part as described in section 4.5.1 of the RDS documentation.

sections.heading: Incomplete workouts and maximum recovery period
sections.text: Future recoveries of the 1,828 incomplete processes are estimated from the recovery patterns of closed processes with the same time in default, segment and workout phase, using the 25th percentile pattern for bankruptcy cases; back-testing on processes closed in 2025–2026 shows estimated recoveries of 96.4% of realised recoveries, and the residual uncertainty is covered by MoC A3. Incomplete processes enter the LRA with these estimated recoveries, so LGD is based on all defaults in the RDS. The maximum recovery period of 72 months (EJ-LGDS-04) is supported by the observed pace of recoveries and consistent with bankruptcy proceedings in the Netherlands.

sections.heading: Calibration
sections.text: The long-run average LGD of each pool is the default-weighted arithmetic average of realised LGDs of all RDS defaults in the pool, including estimated future recoveries; yearly averages are not used. Realised LGDs reflecting a profit are set to zero for observed and long-run average LGD, while unfloored values are used in the haircut estimation. The LRA LGD is 27.7% overall: 15.2% for real estate secured, 31.8% for other secured and 44.6% for unsecured facilities; calibration is tested at pool and segment level, and no pool shows significant underestimation. Estimates rely on the Bank's own loss experience and not on market prices, and are representative of long-run experience including the 2012–2014 downturn.

sections.heading: Identification of the economic downturn
sections.text: The economic downturn for the type of exposures 'retail SME' was identified in January 2027 under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/930, separately from other types of exposures. The relevant indicator set comprises GDP, the unemployment rate, CBS business bankruptcies as external default rate, DNB write-offs on SME loans as external credit loss, value added of the five material sector groups, the MSCI commercial property capital value and rental value indices, and the CBS house price index for residential collateral of entrepreneurs. Sector value added is included separately per material sector group, because the sectors did not co-move strongly (hospitality and construction reached their troughs in different years), so a common indicator is not used. GDP, value added and property indices are analysed in 12-month changes, unemployment in levels, and bankruptcies and write-offs in 12-month sums. For each indicator the most severe 12-month value over the 20 years ending December 2025 was determined, considering periods starting in any month; the span was assessed as representative because it includes the 2009 recession, the 2013 bankruptcy peak and the 2020 pandemic shock, and was not extended.

sections.heading: Downturn periods
sections.text: Most severe values: GDP −9.1% and hospitality value added −38.6% (12 months to June 2020); construction value added −10.2% (12 months to June 2010); unemployment 7.5% (to February 2014); bankruptcies, SME write-offs, retail trade value added and commercial property capital (−8.9%) and rental values (to December 2013 and March 2014). The correlated indicators peaking in 2013–2014 are merged into one downturn period DP-B from April 2012 to March 2014, which covers all related peaks and is extended because bankruptcies remained within 10% of their peak throughout 2013. GDP and hospitality form DP-A (July 2019–June 2020), and construction forms DP-C (July 2009–June 2010), each equal to the 12-month period of the most severe value. The periods are based on observed conditions, not on stress scenarios, reflect cyclical effects and are reviewed annually and when new information arises.

sections.heading: Downturn impact analysis and quantification
sections.text: For DP-B the impact analysis shows realised LGD per default year rising from 25.1% (2010) to 31.4% (2012) and 32.8% (2013), cure rates within 24 months falling to 34.6%, time in default rising to 29 months and recovery-to-value of commercial real estate falling to 52%, with a lag of up to 12 months, so that defaults up to March 2015 are attributed to DP-B. For DP-A no impact is observed because of support measures; for DP-C, which precedes the RDS, loss data are insufficient, and the downturn LGD is estimated with an extrapolation approach based on the statistically significant dependency between construction-sector LGL and construction value added (slope 0.84, p < 0.01), with a strictly positive Category A MoC from the 90% confidence interval. For DP-B the components are recalibrated on the defaults of the period, starting with the haircuts, which show the highest impact (downturn haircuts: commercial real estate 46%, residential 31%, receivables 66%, inventory 83%, equipment 72%), then LGL_U and P(cure); recalibration on the same cohort preserves their dependency, and cash flows after 72 months are excluded. Applied to the current portfolio including final MoC, the average downturn LGD is 29.8% for DP-A, 35.0% for DP-B and 31.1% for DP-C; DP-B is selected for all segments, with downturn best estimates of 20.1% (real estate), 37.0% (other secured) and 50.2% (unsecured). Downturn LGD is calibrated at pool level and aggregated to segment level, and the downturn LGD plus MoC exceeds the LRA plus MoC in all segments, so the downturn estimate is used, in accordance with EBA/GL/2019/03 and the requirements of EBA/GL/2017/16, and documented per segment in table 5.3.

sections.heading: Reference value and cyclicality
sections.text: The two default years with the highest ratio of economic loss to outstanding amount are 2013 and 2012, and the reference value per segment (simple average of their average realised LGDs) is 19.4% for real estate, 35.8% for other secured and 49.6% for unsecured, 32.1% overall. The final downturn LGD exceeds the reference value in every segment. Because collateral values and utilisation are cycle-sensitive drivers, the pool distribution of the real estate segment was recalculated with DP-B property values; 18% of EAD would move to higher pools, and the pool-level downturn calibration limits the resulting cyclicality.

sections.heading: ELBE, LGD in-default and floors
sections.text: An ELBE and LGD in-default are assigned to every defaulted exposure, estimated per reference date in default (0, 6, 12, 24, 36, 48 months and bankruptcy declaration) from realised LGDs at that reference date. The ELBE contains no MoC and reflects current circumstances through the current collateral values and workout phase; the LGD in-default adds a downturn component, inferred from the DP-B calibration per reference date, and the MoC. LGD in-default exceeds the ELBE for all exposures and is raised where the specific credit risk adjustment exceeds it; at 31 December 2026 the ELBE averages 38.2% and the LGD in-default 43.9% for 1,940 defaulted facilities (add-on: 3.6 pp downturn, 2.1 pp MoC). The final performing LGD is floored at exposure level after downturn adjustment and MoC with the input floors of CRR Article 164(4): 30% for the unsecured part and 10% for receivables and immovable property and 15% for other physical collateral on the secured part, combined as in Article 161(6); the floor binds for 9.7% of EAD. The order best estimate, downturn, MoC, floor is identical in development and RCE.

sections.heading: Margin of conservatism
sections.text: The final LGD is the best estimate including appropriate adjustments plus a MoC quantified under CRM-STD-101 in Categories A, B and C. Deficiencies were identified with the trigger list of CRM-STD-101 Annex 1, including those considered and rejected (DD-LGDS-04), and an appropriate adjustment was considered first for each. Each deficiency is linked to one category and recorded in the MoC register with identifier, affected segments and reference to the data deficiency log; deficiencies found by validation, monitoring, audit or supervision are added within three months. A1 default flag approximation: +0.4 pp in all segments (60-dpd alternative); A2 migrated collateral data: +0.5, +0.8 and 0.0 pp (range of valuation-date alternatives); A3 incomplete workouts: +0.4, +0.6, +0.5 pp; B1 WHOA: +0.3, +0.4, +0.5 pp; B2 BMKB scheme changes: +0.1, +0.1, +0.2 pp. Each deficiency is quantified per segment before aggregation, is non-negative and not lower than the adverse sensitivity result, and favourable effects do not offset other components; no expert judgement was needed for quantification.

sections.heading: Category C and aggregation
sections.text: Category C MoC is the difference between the 90th percentile of the bootstrapped LRA (5,000 replications, resampling defaulted facilities, seed 20270301) and the LRA: 0.25, 0.55 and 0.45 pp for the three segments. The total MoC per segment is the simple sum of Categories A, B and C: 1.95 pp (real estate), 2.85 pp (other secured) and 2.05 pp (unsecured), added to the downturn best estimate so that it covers both LRA and downturn uncertainty. The total MoC is below 5 pp, so no redevelopment assessment by the MRC is required, and the RWEA effect of the MoC is EUR 241 million, reported per category.

sections.heading: Discriminatory power, calibration and stability
sections.text: The gAUC is 0.664 on development, 0.659 out-of-sample and 0.648 out-of-time (relative decrease 2.4%), against 0.611 for version 1.4 on the same out-of-time sample; per segment it ranges from 0.611 to 0.672. The model differentiates risk adequately, with drivers forming a reasonable basis and no material bias. On the out-of-time sample, realised LGD of closed cases (24.9%) is below the best estimate (26.3%), and the one-sided paired t-test shows no underestimation in any pool; back-testing is done at component and facility level. Kruskal–Wallis and Mann–Whitney tests confirm homogeneity within and heterogeneity between adjacent pools; pools were merged where not distinct (EJ-LGDS-05). Coefficients re-estimated on 2010–2017 and 2018–2025 defaults are consistent within two standard errors.

sections.heading: Benchmarking and sensitivity
sections.text: As a Tier 2 model, version 2.0 was compared with version 1.4 as benchmark: gAUC 0.648 against 0.611, and final EAD-weighted LGD 30.4% against 31.8% (including the post-model adjustment), the difference being explained by the recognition of receivables, inventory and equipment and the new downturn calibration. In the 2026 supervisory benchmarking under CRD Article 78, the Bank submitted retail SME LGD results with methodology explanations; the Bank's average LGD of 31.8% compared with an EU median of 33.5%. Sensitivity analyses covered maximum recovery period (60 and 84 months: −0.3 and +0.1 pp), discount add-on ±1 pp (±0.6 pp), inventory haircut 74% and 84% (−0.2 and +0.2 pp), calibration window 2013–2025 (−0.5 pp) and the alternative default flag approximations; results support the MoC quantification. The amber PSI of utilisation was analysed and recorded in the limitations log as L-06.

sections.heading: Individual defaults and climate risk
sections.text: For the smallest pools a sample of 50 defaults was reviewed with FR&R to confirm that main loss drivers (ground privilege, fraud, BMKB rejection) are reflected, without adapting the model to singular events. Climate and environmental risks were assessed: energy labels of commercial real estate and sector transition risk showed no significant effect on recoveries in the RDS, so no climate driver is included, and the assessment is repeated annually. The review also confirmed that the model reflects the SME workout practice of FR&R.

sections.heading: Assumptions and limitations
sections.text: Material assumptions: recovery patterns of closed processes apply to incomplete ones; haircuts observed in 2010–2025 remain valid; the BMKB scheme continues; collateral valuations at origination and indexation represent realisable value; the model is used only within its range of application. The model does not work effectively for exposures above EUR 1 million, for collateral located outside the Netherlands, for sectors newly entered by the Bank, or under a WHOA-dominated recovery environment not represented in the RDS. The limitations log (chapter 8.1 of this MDD) states for each entry identifier, description, source, impact, mitigant and owner: L-01 incomplete workouts (MoC A3), L-02 default flag approximation (MoC A1), L-03 migrated collateral data (MoC A2), L-04 indirect costs before 2013, L-05 inventory haircut based on few observations (EJ-LGDS-03), L-06 utilisation shift, L-07 WHOA experience (MoC B1). The log is kept up to date, material limitations are reported to the approval authority at G3 and recorded in the inventory, and they are communicated to users. Approximations used in risk reports based on model outputs are documented here and supported by the back-testing.

sections.heading: Implementation
sections.text: Version 2.0 is implemented in RCE according to implementation specification IS-LGDS-2.0, approved by the model owner on 12 May 2027 and consistent with this MDD; implementation and parallel run are documented in EVD-05-IMPL. The handover package contained the specification, parameter table PT-LGDS-2.0, 860 test cases and reference outputs of the development code. Version 2.0 runs in the shadow environment and will be used for own funds requirements only after ECB permission and after implementation testing, reconciliation, parallel run and UAT. The RCE applies the retail risk weight formula with the model LGD, as tested for version 2.0. Production code, specification and MDD are consistent, which the model owner confirms after each change and at least annually.

sections.heading: Monitoring
sections.text: The monitoring plan, approved by the model owner and reviewed by Model Validation, defines KPIs, calculation, thresholds, frequency, periods, segments, responsibilities and escalation. KPIs: back-testing of realised versus estimated LGD (one-sided t-test, amber p < 5%, red p < 1%; portfolio underestimation above 5% relative amber and 10% red), gAUC decrease (amber above 10%, red above 20%), PSI of pools and drivers (amber 0.10, red 0.25), realised versus predicted cure rates, recovery-to-value per collateral type, BMKB acceptance rate, ELBE back-test, production DQ, overrides and coverage. KPIs are computed for the model, each segment and each pool, semi-annually as required for Tier 2, and reported within 60 days; the plan is updated with every change and reviewed annually. Amber results are analysed and documented; red results or repeated amber are notified to MRM and Model Validation within ten business days with a root cause analysis and action plan within 60 days, proposing no action, overlay, recalibration, redevelopment or restriction, and unresolved triggers after six months go to the MRC. The review-of-estimates framework defines scope, frequency, metrics, thresholds and actions, reviews estimates at least annually, and revises estimates upward where realised values continue to exceed estimates, with a recalibration plan approved by the MRC within three months after a red outcome. The annual review covers representativeness, performance on the whole application portfolio and back-testing per pool, concludes on fitness for purpose, and is provided to Model Validation; monitoring code is versioned in lgd-sme-monitoring.

sections.heading: Expert judgement and overrides
sections.text: Every expert judgement is recorded in the log EJ-LGDS, referenced here, and approved before use: EJ-LGDS-01 default flag approximation (medium), EJ-LGDS-02 collateral type mapping (medium), EJ-LGDS-03 inventory haircut (medium, +0.2 pp), EJ-LGDS-04 maximum recovery period of 72 months (low), EJ-LGDS-05 pool merges (low). Each entry records type, stage, affected parameter, rationale, evidence and alternatives, quantified impact, proposer, approver, dates and expiry conditions, and design judgements are justified in the relevant sections of this MDD. EJ-LGDS-03 was elicited from a panel of five FR&R workout specialists in two Delphi rounds; the panel composition and method are documented, and the aggregate result was set at the median. Medium judgements were independently challenged and approved by the model owner and head of development; the aggregate effect is +0.6 pp (2.0% relative), below the high threshold, and the effect of judgement on performance is negligible. Pool assignment of performing exposures cannot be overridden; FR&R may override collateral values of defaulted exposures only for a closed list of reasons (signed sale agreement, new valuation, confirmed fraud), with the evidence value as maximum and approval by a senior credit officer independent of the case handler, stricter for favourable overrides. Each override is recorded with reason code, rationale, evidence, proposer and approver; override rates (3.4% of defaulted facilities in 2026) are monitored semi-annually and overridden cases analysed annually against pre-override values, including per approving officer. Human oversight by FR&R and credit risk management complements the model and detects errors from model weaknesses.

sections.heading: Purpose and summary
sections.text: This memorandum describes and classifies the change from version 1.4 to version 2.0 of the LGD model for retail SME exposures (MDL-05), in accordance with MRM-STD-050 and Delegated Regulation (EU) No 529/2014. The change was recorded in the change log of the model inventory on 14 September 2026, before any implementation in production. Proposed classification: internally material; regulatory Class A (material change requiring prior permission of the ECB under CRR Article 143(3)). Memorandum version 1.0 of 21 May 2027, prepared by K. Bos, approved by the model owner; classification approved by Model Risk Management on 28 May 2027.

sections.heading: Description and rationale of the change
sections.text: The change package comprises: C1 replacement of the downturn methodology (version 1.4 applies a multiplicative add-on of 1.12 to the LRA) by a downturn identification under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/930 and calibration under EBA/GL/2019/03; C2 recognition of pledges on receivables, inventory and equipment as collateral types in LGD estimation, previously treated as unsecured; C3 modelling of the BMKB guarantee as a recovery component instead of a flat LGD reduction of 8 pp; C4 use of the collateral management system CMS as data source for estimation and pool assignment; C5 extension of the calibration sample from 2010–2021 to 2010–2025; C6 MoC methodology per CRM-STD-101. The rationale is supervisory obligation O-2 of the ECB decision of 12 December 2024 to align the downturn LGD with EBA/GL/2019/03 by 30 June 2028, and validation finding F-2025-LGDS-03 on the unrecognised collateral types. Affected components are the performing LGD, ELBE and LGD in-default, the pool structure (8 pools replaced by 10), the parameter table and the RDS; affected documents are the RDS documentation, MDD, implementation specification and monitoring plan. Because C1 to C6 are planned together and address the same deficiencies, they are recorded and assessed as a single change and not split into changes of lower materiality.

sections.heading: Scope of application and volumes
sections.text: The change affects the entire range of application of the retail SME LGD model: 97,800 facilities, 61,200 obligors, EAD EUR 7.4 billion and RWEA EUR 3,386 million at 31 December 2026; the range of application itself is not extended. Planned implementation date: the first month-end after three months following ECB permission at the latest, expected in the second half of 2028, in line with the expectation to implement within three months of notification of the permission; an exception would be requested with reasons as early as possible. Current version 1.4 and proposed version 2.0 are recorded in the inventory with their version numbers.

sections.heading: Qualitative classification
sections.text: C1 and C6 change the downturn and MoC methodology and C3 the LGD estimation methodology, which are qualitative criteria for material changes under Annex I, Part II, Section 1, point 2(f) of Delegated Regulation (EU) No 529/2014. C2 includes collateral types whose treatment differs from approved procedures, a material change under point 2(g). C4 (change of data source) and C5 (change in time series composition, as the pre-2019 collateral data are remapped) would individually require ex ante notification under Section 2, point 5(b) and 5(c), and are absorbed in the Class A change. The change does not alter the definition of default, the rating philosophy or the validation methodology. Internally, the change is material because it alters methodology, drivers and segmentation, introduces a new input source and is Class A.

sections.heading: Quantitative impact
sections.text: The impact was calculated on the most recent reference date, 31 December 2026, for the same exposure set before and after the change, isolating the effect of the change: RWEA of the range of application decreases from EUR 3,386 million to EUR 3,264 million (−3.6%), and the Bank's overall credit and dilution risk RWEA of EUR 52.6 billion decreases by 0.23%. Neither quantitative threshold for a material change is reached (1.5% at Bank level, 15% for the range of application), and the decrease is below the 5% ex ante notification threshold; the classification as Class A follows from the qualitative criteria. The EAD-weighted LGD changes from 31.8% (including the +2.0 pp post-model adjustment) to 30.4% (−4.4% relative), and 29% of facilities change LGD pool after mapping, above the 10% threshold of MRM-STD-050 section 5.2(e). A precise calculation was feasible on the full portfolio, so no sampling was needed. By component: C1 +2.1 pp, C2 −2.3 pp, C3 −0.4 pp, C5 −0.3 pp, C6 +0.5 pp, removal of the post-model adjustment −2.0 pp.

sections.heading: Cumulative impact and conservatism of classification
sections.text: The cumulative impact of the non-material changes since the last permission (v1.2 to v1.4, 2019–2023) is +2.9% RWEA, so the cumulative assessment does not change the classification. As the qualitative criteria are unambiguous, no classification doubt exists; had there been doubt, the higher category would have been applied. The change policy of the Bank, MRM-STD-050, sets out how changes are identified, classified, approved, documented, notified and implemented, with criteria that ensure a consistent classification free of arbitrage. Since the change is Class A, the next validation after implementation is full scope.

sections.text: As an internally material Class A change, version 2.0 is independently validated before the application is submitted, and the validation report will be part of the application; Model Validation plans a full-scope change validation from 1 July to 30 September 2027. The change passes gates G1 to G4 again; after validation it is approved by the Model Approval Panel as approval authority for the Tier 2 model, and, as it requires supervisory permission, by the Model Risk Committee before submission, planned for October 2027. The application will not be submitted with an open high-severity finding on the changed model unless disclosed and approved by the MRC.

sections.heading: Interim compliance and supervisory obligations
sections.text: Until version 2.0 is implemented, version 1.4 does not fully comply with the downturn requirements; the Bank has notified the ECB, and the plan to restore compliance by 30 June 2028 is monitored by the MRC. As mitigating measure, a post-model adjustment of +2.0 pp on LGD has been applied since 1 January 2025, approved by the Model Approval Panel on 9 December 2024 and reported quarterly to the MRC; it exceeds the estimated shortfall of version 1.4 downturn LGD (1.1 pp). Obligation O-2 is recorded in the inventory with owner (model owner) and deadline, and tracked as MRC condition C-2025-LGDS-01. As the post-model adjustment has been in place for 24 months in January 2027, it triggered the model change assessment under MRM-STD-050 that is concluded by this change. A post-implementation review comparing realised with estimated impact will be performed within six months after implementation and reported to MRM.

Internal Audit covered the SME rating systems in audit IA-2026-009, based on its annual risk assessment of the rating systems. The next validation of version 2.0 is the full-scope change validation planned for July to September 2027.

deficiencies.rationale: The legal opinion on pledges of inventory and equipment covers Dutch law only; 2.3% of other physical collateral is located in Belgium or Germany, for which the jurisdiction of registration and likely realisation is not covered.

mitigation.text: Obtain legal opinions for Belgian and German law or exclude foreign-located other physical collateral from recognition in LGD estimation.

deficiencies.rationale: The comparison of the current pool distribution with the distribution under the downturn period is performed only for the real estate segment; the other secured segment, whose drivers (utilisation, receivables and inventory values) are also cycle-sensitive, is not analysed.

mitigation.text: Extend the cyclicality analysis to the other secured segment and document whether an adjustment of the downturn LGD is required.

deficiencies.rationale: For the inventory haircut set by expert panel (EJ-LGDS-03), panel composition and Delphi method are documented, but the individual contributions and the aggregation of opinions are not.

mitigation.text: Add the individual panel estimates per Delphi round and the aggregation rule to the expert judgement log and the MDD.

deficiencies.rationale: The RDS documentation states that RVO payments are allocated to the covered part of partially guaranteed facilities, but for 2010–2014 legacy cases RVO payments were booked at facility level and the build code allocates them pro rata to covered and uncovered parts, understating the realised LGD of the uncovered part (validation estimate +0.3 pp for BMKB facilities).

mitigation.text: Re-allocate legacy RVO payments to the covered part using the guarantee percentage from the BMKB administration and recalibrate LGL_U; cover the residual uncertainty by MoC.

deficiencies.rationale: Category C MoC is computed with a bootstrap that resamples defaulted facilities, ignoring the clustering of 1.78 facilities per defaulted obligor; an obligor-level bootstrap gives a 90th percentile deviation 0.21 pp higher for the other secured segment, so the MoC understates the estimation error.

mitigation.text: Recompute Category C MoC with an obligor-level (cluster) bootstrap and increase the MoC of the affected segments accordingly.

codeFacts.check: Maximum recovery period used for closure of recovery processes in the RDS build code
codeFacts.detail: rds-lgd-sme rds_build_sme.py L301: MAX_RECOVERY_MONTHS = 84 (documented in RDS §2.3 and MDD §4.6: 72 months).

codeFacts.check: Retail LGD input floors (30% unsecured, 10%/10%/15% secured, Art. 161(6) combination) at exposure level after downturn and MoC
codeFacts.detail: rce-lgd-sme floors.py L40–71: floor = (E_U*0.30 + sum(E_S_c*floor_c))/EAD applied after lgd_dt + moc; binding for 9.7% of EAD, as documented in MDD §5.5.
rds-lgd-sme discounting.py L33: rate = euribor_3m_at_default + 0.05, EURIBOR used as observed (documented: same).

validationTests.detail: RDS rebuilt independently from BLP, SAMS, RECOV, CMS and GL: 21,698 default events reproduced; realised LGD per event within 0.02 pp, except the closure status of 146 processes affected by the recovery period parameter.
Code-versus-documentation: rds_build_sme.py L301 uses a maximum recovery period of 84 months instead of the documented 72; 146 processes remain open longer, LRA effect −0.1 pp.
Downturn LGD best estimate per segment (20.1% / 37.0% / 50.2%) is not lower than the realised LGD of DP-B defaults (19.6% / 36.1% / 49.8%).
Category C MoC reproduced with the developer's facility-level bootstrap; an obligor-level cluster bootstrap yields +0.21 pp higher MoC for the other secured segment.
gAUC on the out-of-time sample 0.648 vs 0.664 at development (relative decrease 2.4%, green); version 1.4 on the same sample 0.611.
